title: EDRi-gram, 19 November 2026
text:
Do you want to receive all the latest news from the digital rights world?

SUBSCRIBE NOW TO THE EDRi-GRAM!

Dear supporters,
Last week, the European Commission put digital fairness on the menu with a proposal for its long-awaited Digital Fairness Act (DFA) – and we have some food for thought.
This law will strengthen consumer protection against manipulative and exploitative commercial practices, such as fake notifications designed to keep bringing us back to an app, endless scrolling that keeps us online way longer than you intended, and other personalised techniques used by online services that exploit our vulnerabilities. First things first, proposal actually takes some important steps forward by introducing new prohibitions on deceptive design, extending specific protections beyond the biggest online platforms, and recognising the harms associated with addictive digital features. However, we were left wondering – why promise digital fairness yet leave the users to do all the work instead of holding manipulative online services responsible? Read our analysis on Tech Policy Press.
Despite it all, the DFA proposal – something that actually might protect our rights online – is a welcome respite in the current wave of deregulation in the EU. This week, we’re also reckoning with the fact that November 19, 2026 marks one year since the Commission published the proposals for the Digital Omnibus. We, along with many other civil society organisations, had warned that this would be a massive reopening of EU’s core digital protections that would risk dismantling the very foundation of human rights and tech policy in the EU. One year on, it seems like we were granted Apollo’s gift of prophecy. On this unfortunate occasion, we’re standing strong with 100 organisations, experts, academics and more to urge EU lawmakers to not simplify away our rights.
In this edition, you can also explore our extremely thorough guide to the European Parliament’s 1840 amendments to the Digital Omnibus on Data, focusing on what they would mean for privacy, data protection and, ultimately, people’s rights. Yes, 1840, you read that right. Hungry for more? Also read our thoughts on the EU governments’ position on the Digital Omnibus.

title: New report documents authoritarian use of technology across the globe
text:
Skip to content

Close

Search

How would you best describe that thing you're looking for?

What is the authoritarian use of technology?
EDRi-member Privacy International (PI) have been observing and monitoring an increase in states’ adoption of authoritarian practices and policies. These practices are facilitated by new and emerging technologies or embodied in their very deployment to stifle dissent, assert control and diminish human rights. These digital technologies, such as facial recognition, social media monitoring, spyware, and more, are being deployed — both online and offline — by authoritarian and democratic regimes alike. PI have coined the term ‘authoritarian use of technology’ to describe this global phenomenon.
PI believes that the authoritarian use of technology goes beyond the unlawful use or abuse of technologies by states that the organisation has been monitoring and exposing for years. Authoritarian use of tech results in a systematic undermining of democratic principles, erosion of the rule of law, exertion of significant social and political control, or normalisation of the surveillance of individuals and their communities – particularly those already at risk.
These technologies are being expanded and entrenched with the purpose of exerting control over entire populations and groups of people at risk, such as human rights defenders (HRDs), journalists, lawyers, activists, dissidents and those from minority ethnic, national and religious backgrounds. This is being done to target, persecute or ostracise them. This ultimately creates a ‘chilling effect’, spreading a fear of reprisal, which serves not only to infringe upon the rights of certain individuals, but of whole communities and populations. In turn, this has a corrosive effect on democratic institutions, mechanisms of accountability, oversight and redress, and the fabric of open societies.
What technologies are being deployed?
In their new report, PI examine the use of five technologies: facial recognition technology, mobile phone extraction, spyware, social media and intelligence monitoring, and mass communications surveillance. The report also provides several cross-cutting themes emerging from the authoritarian use of these technologies on human rights. These include: a systemic interference with the right to privacy, the erosion of and chilling effect on enjoyment of broader fundamental rights and freedoms, the disproportionate or discriminatory targeting of certain groups in society, the absence of clear legal basis, effective safeguards, and independent oversight, and lastly, the lack of accountability of private sector actors.
Facial recognition technology (FRT) is a technology that uses a camera to capture images of people’s faces and then extracts and processes their biometric data to verify an individual or identify a match against an existing image. The report collates examples of how governments and law enforcement are deploying FRT at protests to identify, monitor and track protesters either openly or surreptitiously, and even banning wearing face coverings at protests to facilitate it. The report also features case studies of FRT projects in the UK, Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territories, and Brazil.
PI’s report includes a chapter on mobile phone extraction, which documents the technology being deployed to gather information and intelligence about activists, journalists, political dissidents, and migrants, which they believe to constitute an authoritarian use of the technology. Our electronic devices, such as our mobile phones and tablets, contain huge amounts of information and sensitive data about our lives. Mobile phone extraction involves extracting data from an individual’s device, or from the cloud services they use, including device information, photos, videos, audio recordings, notes, documents and apps used, as well as the messages, call logs and emails they draft, send and receive.
The report also gathers examples of […]

title: EU transforms Frontex into a high-tech deportation command centre
text:
Skip to content

Close

Search

How would you best describe that thing you're looking for?

Frontex as an ICE-style deportation enforcement agency
At the centre of this reform is a budget that would almost double to nearly €12 billion for 2028–2034, leading to a massive expansion of the EU security and surveillance industrial complex. Frontex will test and deploy new technology to repress migrants, funnelling billions of taxpayer money to surveillance, security and defence contractors. EU’s hostile border security regime has for years produced systemic and massive human rights violations of migrants, refugees and racialised people, and those who stand in solidarity with them. This proposal will accelerate that.
The proposal operationalises the recently adopted Deportations Regulation and deepens Frontex’s position as the central actor of a Europe-wide deportation machine. This will make the agency responsible for collecting and analysing data from Member States in order to “predict” deportation needs, and allocating resources to them. Frontex will now have a “Deportation Coordination Centre” that is expected to act at all stages of the deportation procedure, from detecting and identifying people that may be expulsed, booking or arranging flights and escorts, to monitoring their “reintegration” in the destination country.
Alarmingly, it expands Frontex’s powers to deport outside of the EU’s borders. Based on a simple status agreement, Frontex will be able to deport people from one third country to another, with the aim of preventing people from even reaching the EU. This will likely mean sharing sensitive data with third countries and countries of origin, where individuals may be at risk of persecution or harm.
The Frontex mandate reform comes in a package with a proposal to digitalise the management of deportation cases. The border control agency is given a key role in the harmonised technical design of EU and national digital systems, to exchange data on deportations, including sensitive data transfers to third countries (biometric data, travel documents and history, grounds for deportation, health data, etc.), and automate certain steps of the procedure, such as adding deportation orders in the Schengen Information System (SIS) to detect people.
Increased data processing and content policing
With this reform, Frontex’s practice of “debriefing interviews” is codified, particularly during the screening procedure introduced by the Migration Pact. The agency conducts these covert “voluntary” interrogations of people immediately after they disembark or cross the border. During these interviews, the agency extracts data from migrants deemed to be “suspects” of “cross-border crime”, without the possibility for migrants to seek legal counsel. Debriefing interviews have been rightfully criticised for their absence of fundamental rights monitoring and their unfairness as they take place when a person is detained and lacks privacy.
A new “Online Monitoring and Response Centre” will also surveil social media platforms to identify “suspicious behaviours or trends” in people’s movements at the EU borders, and before that, in the countries of origin and transit. Aggregated data collected online will be fed into Frontex’s “risk analysis” to guide border forces’ deployment and reaction. Social media monitoring was already declared as carrying high-risk for violating the fundamental rights of people affected, and was banned by the European Data Protection Supervisor in 2019 when first implemented by the EU Agency for Asylum.
Frontex will also seek designation as a trusted flagger under the Digital Services Act (DSA), allowing the agency to report pieces of online content to platforms for removal, effectively giving the agency extrajudicial powers to police the internet. It may also recommend national authorities to issue binding take-down notices. Frontex depriving people from finding legal support, sharing their stories or expressing […]

title: One year later, a broad coalition tells EU lawmakers: do not simplify away people’s rights with the Digital Omnibus
text:
Skip to content

Close

Search

How would you best describe that thing you're looking for?

Simplification cannot mean fewer rights
A new open letter calls on EU lawmakers to protect data protection, privacy and other fundamental rights, rather than weakening them in the name of empty promises of competitiveness and the AI hype.
There are plenty of things about EU digital regulation that could genuinely be simpler: people should not have to fight through endless cookie banners, regulators should cooperate better, businesses should not operate in good faith knowing other companies won’t be held accountable when disrespecting the law…
But cutting red tape and cutting rights are not the same thing. The Digital Omnibus proposed, amongst other, significant changes to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy framework. These affect when information about us is protected, how companies may reuse personal data for AI, safeguards around automated decision-making, access and transparency rights, and protection against unwanted access to our devices.
All of this is happening in a much wider political context. Across different EU policy areas, protections for people, workers, consumers and the environment are increasingly being reopened and deregulated under the language of ‘simplification’ and competitiveness.
The AI data grab is only part of the story
One of the clearest examples is AI. Companies developing AI systems want enormous amounts of data. The Digital Omnibus on Data would create a specific route under the GDPR for AI development, training and operation to rely on the so-called legitimate interest legal basis. The existing legal tests would not disappear, but the risk is that large-scale reuse of personal data for AI becomes increasingly normalised, while people are left to find out what happened to their data and try to object afterwards.
This is particularly concerning in a market already dominated by big tech companies with huge advantages in data, infrastructure and capital, which can undermine companies that have invested in more privacy-protective and rights-respecting products and want clear rules and a genuine level playing field.
AI is only one piece of the proposal. Other changes touch sensitive and biometric data, automated decisions, transparency and access rights, and the confidentiality of our devices and communications.
This is not just a ‘privacy activists’ debate
These changes matter differently to different communities. They matter to workers subject to automated management and surveillance, worried about losing their jobs or their tasks becoming even more alienating; patients whose sensitive information needs strong protection; people facing discrimination who rely on transparency and access rights to challenge unfair systems; journalists and human rights defenders who depend on confidential communications; children and young people exposed to commercial tracking; and consumers confronted with companies holding vastly more information and power than they do.
That is why this cannot be treated as a niche dispute, even less when we remember the GDPR is the cornerstone of the EU’s digital rulebook.
One year on, there is still time to change course
To mark the first, and hopefully last, anniversary of the proposal, 100 organisations, academics, researchers, individuals and responsible businesses are coming together around a simple message: the EU can simplify its rules without simplifying away people’s rights.
The open letter calls on the European Parliament and Member States to reject provisions that weaken rights and substantive protections, and to ensure that any evidence-backed genuine problems in the GDPR, ePrivacy or other legislation are addressed through proper democratic processes, backed by evidence, consultation and scrutiny.
Fundamental rights are not red tape, and if we are speaking about simplification, the question should rather be ‘simplification for whom?’

title: Plan Before the Panic | How to Avoid Scams as a Family
text: Introduction | The Call Every Family Should Plan ForYour phone rings, and the voice sounds just like your child. “Mom, it’s me. I’m in trouble, and I need money right now. Please don’t tell Dad.” Your heart races before your mind catches up. The same panic can start with a text from a “new number” or a warning that your computer has a virus. That reaction is what scammers count on, so the best protection is a family plan made before a message like this comes.Events like International Fraud Awareness Week and year-end family gatherings are good reminders to start that conversation. Here is how to talk about scams across generations without blame, spot common digital scams, set up a family code word, and respond if someone you love is scammed.Why Scams Are a Conversation for Every GenerationScams are a problem for every generation. In a 2025 survey of 46,000 adults across 42 markets by the Global Anti-Scam Alliance and Feedzai, 23% reported losing money to a scam, with those figures coming in at 27% among Gen Z and 26% among Millennials.Research also shows the risks shift with age. The FTC’s latest report on older consumers found that Americans 60 and over reported losing money less often than younger adults in 2025, but their median losses were much higher. They were also more likely to report losing money to scams impersonating friends or family.As our partner, Take9, points out, Millennials and Gen X are often responsible for the digital safety of both their children and their parents. That is a lot to carry alone, which is why the conversation should go both ways.Digital Scams to Talk About With Every GenerationNot every scam starts with a phone call. The Global Anti-Scam Alliance report notes that younger generations, who are more likely to shop online and see investment “opportunities” on social media, are especially at risk. GCA’s guide to safer online shopping covers the warning signs of online shopping scams.Older adults face investment scams too. The FTC found that their reported losses to investment scams jumped 42% in 2025 to over $1 billion, often after scammers reached out to them on social media. They were also more likely than younger adults to report losing money to tech support scams, where scammers try to get remote access to a computer. The Seraph Secure tool in our toolkit can find and remove unwanted remote access tools.How to Talk About Scams With Your Family Without BlameStart with “us” not “you.” Mentioning a suspicious text you received or a scam in the news makes the topic feel shared instead of pointed at one person. Ask what they have seen and listen first. Parents and grandparents may have hard-won instincts about pressure tactics, and often their kids or grandkids can help set up multi-factor authentication.Give everyone permission to be skeptical. As Kitboga, who started fighting scams to protect people like his grandparents, told GCA in a Global Voices interview, “I don’t think that it’s rude to be skeptical.” Express to your family members and loved ones that hanging up on an unexpected call is always okay, even when the caller sounds like family. You can always call them back yourself (using a number that you know belongs to them). Gen Z adults may feel confident because they grew up online, but the research above shows they lose money more often than average. CyberFlex gives young adults ages 18 to 25 a free space to learn about scams and share experiences.How to Set Up a Family Code WordCriminals can use AI to clone a voice from a short audio clip, one of the risks in our guide to deepfakes. In GCA’s 2026 Consumer Cyber Readiness Report with Consumer Reports and Aspen Digital, about a third of U.S. respondents whose most recent scam attempt began with a phone call said it was personalized to them.A family code word adds an extra check. The FBI recommends creating “a secret word or phrase with your family to verify their identity,” and Age UK suggests agreeing on a “safe phrase” with close […]

CVE-2026-77312 - Flyto2 Core: Arbitrary file write via unguarded data.*/file.* modules (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-67429)
text:
10.0

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-77312
Flyto2 Core: Arbitrary file write via unguarded data.*/file.* modules (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-67429)

Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, the earlier CVE-2026-67429 remediation applied validate_path_with_env_config() to only a hand-picked set of file-writing modules, leaving data.csv.write in src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py, data.json_to_csv in src/core/modules/atomic/data/json_to_csv.py, file.copy in src/core/modules/atomic/file/copy.py, and file.move in src/core/modules/atomic/file/move.py outside the FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR confinement boundary. The advisory also identifies unguarded modules across the broader data.*, file.*, and report-writer families. data.csv.write relies on a .. substring denylist that does not reject absolute paths, while the other named modules accept caller-controlled output or destination paths without the canonical guard. A caller able to execute modules or recipes can therefore write attacker-controlled content outside the configured sandbox, potentially overwriting application code, recipes, startup files, scheduled-task files, or authorization files and gaining code execution on the host. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

title: CVE-2026-133476 - Dolibarr SQL Injection Vulnerability
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-133476
Dolibarr SQL Injection Vulnerability

In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, dolForgeSQLCriteriaCallback() in htdocs/core/lib/functions.lib.php allows account takeover because it strips only a single table-name prefix from a Universal Search Filter (sqlfilters) operand before checking it against the forbidden-field denylist (pass, pass_crypted, api_key). MariaDB and MySQL accept a two-level qualification such as schema.alias.column, so an operand of the form dolibarr.u.pass_crypted survives the check and is emitted into the WHERE clause. A remote authenticated user holding only the holiday read and readall permissions, which confer no user-management or administrative access, can use the resulting boolean oracle at GET /api/index.php/holidays to recover any user's bcrypt password hash and api_key one character at a time, including an administrator's. Because api_key is accepted directly by the REST API as a bearer credential, this yields full administrative control of the application. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-89012, which added only a strtolower() call and did not address prefix depth. The same denylist also omits pass_temp, which stores a password in cleartext, as well as national_registration_number, salary, birth, address, personal_mobile and note_private.

title: CVE-2026-130179 - Credential Overwriting in Okta .NET SDK Abstractions Library
text:
8.5

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-130179
Credential Overwriting in Okta .NET SDK Abstractions Library

The Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library systematically writes per-request authentication credentials to a shared HTTP client instance, rather than being isolated to individual outbound request objects. When using scoped child clients, a subsequent scoped request can overwrite the shared client configuration. Because the original parent client credential has not been restored, subsequent outbound requests may be transmitted using the newly written credential, which can result in subsequent actions being executed under the context of an incorrect security principal in the Okta Management API and improper attribution in audit logs.

title: CVE-2026-129932 - Attacker able to redirect a Java driver client to a host they own, surviving TLS certificate verification, via an SRV parent-domain bypass
text:
9.1

CRITICAL
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-129932
Attacker able to redirect a Java driver client to a host they own, surviving TLS certificate verification, via an SRV parent-domain bypass

The MongoDB Java driver applies its DNS seedlist domain restriction to a record value that is later re-interpreted differently when the connection target is parsed, so the name that is checked and the name that is used can differ. An unauthenticated party who can set or forge the DNS service record for the seed domain in a connection string can cause the driver to direct its session to an unrelated host and to complete certificate verification against that host instead. This may result in unintended disclosure of application data and of configured database credentials, and in unintended content being returned to the application as query results.

title: CVE-2026-76540 - Improper Authorization through the REST API in Splunk Enterprise
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-76540
Improper Authorization through the REST API in Splunk Enterprise

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 9.4.17, 10.0.12, 10.2.9, and 10.4.5, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles can configure a metric alert through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API that runs a search with elevated privileges. The vulnerability lets the user access or modify data and disrupt the Splunk Enterprise instance.
The vulnerability occurs because Splunk Enterprise does not enforce the required role-based authorization when it processes metric alert configuration through the REST API. Splunk Enterprise schedules the resulting search with elevated authorization and runs attacker-controlled search processing with that authorization.
For more information see About configuring role-based user access (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/about-configuring-role-based-user-access) in the Splunk documentation.

title: Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era
text: Fahmida Y. Rashid,Editor-in-Chief,Dark ReadingNovember 19, 2026 The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month, it was PHP2Shell. This week, it's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by Calif Research, and NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by Rapid7 MDR.In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei, Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones, and Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid discuss last month's PHP2Shell vulnerability and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging AI would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched. However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophe can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.A similar wave of urgency currently surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it. A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical and operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.David Jones, Alissa Irei, Fahmida Y. Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): CrowdStrike Detects Exposure and Post-Exploitation Activity

CVE-2026-114938, dubbed "Java4Shell," is a memory corruption vulnerability in the HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), the runtime shared by Oracle Java SE, OpenJDK, and many downstream Java distributions. 
Although HotSpot is widely deployed, exposure to this vulnerability is narrower than its footprint suggests. Exploitation requires three conditions: an affected Java version, x86-64 hardware that supports AVX-512 VBMI, and an application that decodes attacker-supplied Base64 data. Even when all three are met, the limited size of the memory overwrite makes reliable remote code execution difficult, though not impossible. 
Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026. Organizations should patch systems that meet all three conditions immediately, starting with internet-facing Java services. Remaining Java deployments can be addressed through regular scheduled patching.
Oracle rates the vulnerability 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. Red Hat rates it 9.8 (Critical) under CVSS 3.0. Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026.

The flaw resides in HotSpot's AVX-512-optimized Base64 decoding routine, a performance shortcut the JVM uses only on processors that support AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI). Base64 is everywhere in modern applications. It carries credentials in HTTP Basic authentication headers, encodes JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) and SAML assertions, and wraps file uploads and binary API payloads. As a result, the vulnerable code path is frequently reachable from untrusted input before any application-level validation takes place.
What elevates this vulnerability is its placement in the stack. The defect sits in the runtime itself, rather than an application, framework, or library. An application that decodes attacker-supplied Base64 using the standard Java class library is exposed even if its own code is flawless. Because the vulnerable code lives in shared HotSpot code, exposure extends beyond Oracle-branded Java. It includes OpenJDK builds from multiple vendors, applications that bundle their own Java runtime, container images, and managed cloud services. 
Java4Shell also has meaningful constraints. The vulnerable code path is only active on specific x86-64 hardware, and the size of the out-of-bounds write is limited. 
An unauthenticated remote attacker who can pass a specially crafted Base64 string to an affected application can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write of up to 62 bytes. Because the overflow lands on the Java heap, its consequences depend on what sits adjacent to the destination buffer when the write occurs. These may include:
Denial of service: Corrupting object headers or JVM metadata causes the JVM to crash. This would be the most likely outcome.Memory disclosure ("JavaBleed"): Under certain conditions, corruption of adjacent object state can cause the application to return heap contents it should not. This could include fragments of other requests, session tokens, or credentials.Remote code execution: Achieving code execution requires the attacker to influence heap layout precisely enough that the limited overwrite corrupts a security-relevant structure, such as an object header, array length, or reference, in a way that can be leveraged further. The 62-byte ceiling, hardware dependency, and variability of heap layout across […]

title: phpAfterShell Explained: How Hackers Could Turn a PHP Session Flaw Into Code Execution
text:
phpAfterShell Explained: How Hackers Could Turn a PHP Session Flaw Into Code ExecutionSwati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

PHP's default file-based session storage can be made to return objects an attacker chose, by cutting off a session write at the right moment. When combined with a second weakness, such as a suitable gadget chain in the app, those objects can allow the attacker to run code on the server.

Today's PHP releases fix the flaw, called phpAfterShell.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-126714 and rated 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 scale by PHP's maintainers. Depthfirst, a security company, says it found the flaw and reported it to the maintainers.

The October 21 PHP releases, which fixed two critical flaws known as PHP2Shell, do not contain this fix. Servers updated then remain affected until they install today's releases. Neither the maintainers nor the company reports any attacks using phpAfterShell.

Who Is Affected and What to Do

These releases are affected, according to the maintainers' security advisory:

Branch

Affected releases

Fixed release

PHP 8.2

Before 8.2.36

8.2.36

PHP 8.3

Before 8.3.37

8.3.37

PHP 8.4

Before 8.4.28

8.4.28

PHP 8.5

Before 8.5.13

8.5.13

PHP 8.6.0, also released today, includes the fix.

The flaw is in the files session handler, which PHP uses by default. Sessions kept in Redis, a database, or another store are outside this defect, though each store's handling of a cut-off update needs its own check.

Whether an attacker needs to log in depends on how the app exposes its session handling.

On the path the company tested, the attacker uses upload progress, a PHP feature that records the progress of a file upload in the user's session. Where the feature is on, a multipart form upload that carries its field makes PHP write to the session before the app's own code runs. The app does not need an upload page, only any page that opens the session later.

PHP 8.1 and older are end-of-life. The official end-of-life mitigation branches for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are not affected, but older unpatched builds of those versions are, according to the company.

The company's remediation guidance sets out these steps:

Install the fixed release for your branch, as listed above. If you run PHP 8.1 or older, move to a supported branch.
Rebuild any container images and redeploy.
Check that the PHP version serving web requests is the new one.

If you cannot update yet and your app does not use upload progress, set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the server's PHP settings, then restart the PHP workers. Also limit the untrusted data your app stores in sessions.

Switching the feature off is not a full fix. It closes the upload path, but apps that put attacker-controlled data into sessions in other ways remain affected, the maintainers say.

The maintainers listed the same setting on October 21 as a temporary measure for one of the PHP2Shell flaws. Servers that have kept it off since then still need the update.

Moving sessions to a store that replaces records in one step also avoids this defect. The update is still the recommended fix for sites that keep the files handler.

Linux distribution packages may include the fix without changing the PHP version number, according to the company, so the version number alone may not indicate whether a server is fixed.

Once installed, the fixed releases empty the session file before each write and stop the write if that step fails. A cut-off write can still lose session data, but it can no longer leave old data behind for an attacker to use.

The updates also switch upload progress off by default. The Hacker News compared PHP's source code for the October 21 releases and today's. The built-in setting is on in 8.2.35, […]

title: PHP Fixes 7 Critical Flaws, Including Bugs That Could Allow Remote Code Execution
text:
PHP Fixes 7 Critical Flaws, Including Bugs That Could Allow Remote Code ExecutionRavie LakshmananNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

The PHP Foundation has released security updates to address multiple critical security flaws that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution on affected deployments, including CVE-2026-115560.

The release of the patch follows an advance notice in which the project maintainers alerted users to multiple critical vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions under specific conditions, including non-default configuration or uncommon setups.

At a high level, successful exploitation of the defects could pave the way for remote code execution, session corruption, denial-of-service, memory corruption, or local privilege escalation.

The list of vulnerabilities is as follows -

CVE-2026-115560 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could result in remote code execution, file modification, session corruption, or denial-of-service. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)
CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in memory corruption and possible full remote code execution, as in the case of CVE-2026-109619. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0)
CVE-2026-126714 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability that could result in the execution of arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker. Successful exploitation requires an attacker's influence over the session data, an interruption at a useful point in the write, and an application with a suitable deserialization gadget chain. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)
CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An inconsistent interpretation of HTTP requests vulnerability that could result in execution of attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker without another user's interaction or a non-default PHP configuration. Successful exploitation requires a front end that enables persistent backend connections and an application path that opens "php://input" without reading it fully, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, HAProxy FastCGI applications that retain backend connections, and LSAPI. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)
CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in remote code execution on PHP 8.5 and later. Successful exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0)
CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could cause an application's session cleanup to fail and potentially corrupt memory, crash a reused PHP worker, or potentially allow remote code execution. (Fixed in PHP 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)
CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code with their privileges on an affected deployment. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)
CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in local privilege escalation. Successful exploitation requires local code execution in an FPM worker, an affected pool with catch_workers_output enabled, the epoll event backend, and the ability to manipulate worker lifetimes and retain inherited pipe descriptors. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

title: Critical VMware vCenter Flaw (CVSS 9.8) Lets Network Attackers Bypass Authentication
text:
Critical VMware vCenter Flaw (CVSS 9.8) Lets Network Attackers Bypass AuthenticationSwati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an advisory published today.

Fixed versions are out for all supported branches, and the company lists no workaround. vCenter is the central console for managing an organization's ESX hosts and virtual machines.

The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123890 and is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service," the advisory says.

In an FAQ published with the advisory, the company says the issue "qualifies under ITIL methodologies as an emergency change," and urges organizations to consult their security staff immediately on timing.

The company has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, or any public exploit code. It also does not say what level of access an attacker gains after the bypass. Credit for reporting the bug goes to Google-owned Mandiant.

The bug is present in vCenter 8.0, 9.0, and 9.1, and in the vCenter builds that ship inside VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and the Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure products. That includes the older Cloud Foundation 5.x line. It is there whether or not Enhanced Linked Mode is in use.

Older versions are not cleared. The company no longer evaluates versions past end of support, and says vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 should be presumed affected. The same goes for vSphere 7.0, which left general support in October 2025, and whose customers can request a patch under an extended support contract.

None of the five flaws in the advisory lets code run on an ESX host from inside a virtual machine, and ESX itself is not affected, the advisory FAQ says.

There is no fallback for systems that cannot be updated yet: asked whether a workaround exists, the FAQ answers "Not as listed by Broadcom," while noting that mitigations may still exist in an organization's own defenses.

The updates are cumulative and cannot be installed through vCenter Quick Patch. Virtual machines continue running while vCenter installs the update, though management access drops briefly, and some encryption operations against a Standard Key Provider become unavailable until vCenter is back online.

One warning applies to upgrades already in progress: installing vCenter 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 blocks a later upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1, a conflict the FAQ calls a "Back-in-Time" issue. The options are to upgrade vCenter to 9.1.1 first and apply the security update there, or to wait briefly for VCF 9.1.2.

The bypass is the second critical authentication flaw in the VMware Directory Service this year. The earlier vCenter flaws, patched on July 29, included CVE-2026-59309, another 9.8-rated bypass in the same component per the July advisory, alongside a directory-traversal bug, CVE-2026-59310.

Attacks on that traversal flaw began five days after its disclosure, German incident response firm QUIRSO assessed in August, linking them with moderate confidence to a suspected China-nexus actor.

The August attacks compromised an estimated 361 IP addresses in 47 countries and deployed Babuk-derived ransomware on ESXi hosts. Broadcom has reported no attacks on the new bypass.

The advisory also fixes four lower-severity flaws, rated 6.7 to 8.1: a SQL injection (CVE-2026-123891) and a command injection (CVE-2026-123892) in SDDC Manager, a privilege escalation to root on the SDDC Manager appliance (CVE-2026-123893), and a SAML token signature bypass in VMware Tools for Windows […]

title: Drupal Patches Critical Installer Flaw That Could Give Unauthenticated Attackers Control of Sites
text:
Drupal Patches Critical Installer Flaw That Could Give Unauthenticated Attackers Control of SitesSwati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site.

That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the project rates the vulnerable configurations as uncommon. Fixed releases for all supported branches shipped yesterday.

The Drupal Security Team disclosed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, yesterday and rated it critical, 18 out of 25 on the project's risk scale.

The installer ships in every copy of Drupal core as the file /core/install.php and stays on the site after installation. Core's default .htaccess rules do not block requests to it, so blocking it is left to each site.

No attacks are reported in the security advisory, which rates exploitation as complex and records an existing proof-of-concept exploit. Some exploit paths are blocked where the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php.

The team had told site owners in an advance notice earlier this week to set aside time for the update, warning that exploits may be developed within hours or days.

Every release below 10.6.22 is affected, along with Drupal 11 releases from 11.0.0 before 11.3.22 and from 11.4.0 before 11.4.13.

What to Do Now

The fixed versions, detailed in the project's release notes, are:

Drupal 11.4.x: update to 11.4.13
Drupal 11.3.x: update to 11.3.22
Drupal 10.6.x: update to 10.6.22

The team recommends blocking the installer even after updating. Sites that cannot update yet should follow the project's installer guidance, updated yesterday, which describes three options: a deny rule in the web server configuration, an .htaccess rule, or removing the file and keeping it removed with Composer scripts.

Sites that use the Drupal Steward protection service are already protected from known attack vectors, according to the team, and should still update in case new vectors emerge.

Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The 11.3.x branch and Drupal 10 lose security coverage altogether in December under the project's support schedule.

In the week of November 8, 154,485 of the 528,430 sites reporting usage data to drupal.org, about 29 percent, were running end-of-life branches.

The flaw was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, an automated service the AI company launched on October 8 to look for vulnerabilities in open-source projects that opt in. Findings go to maintainers without human review, each with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch, according to its launch announcement.

Drupal's security team said on November 2 that a surge of security reports, which it attributes to AI tools, is more than it can sustain at its current funding, and that it is cutting security coverage for core minor versions from 12 months to 8 starting in 2027.

This is the second critical remote code execution flaw fixed in Drupal core in two months, after the Field UI flaw patched on October 14, which also had at least one exploit path that needed no login.

title: Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall
text:
Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your FirewallThe Hacker NewsNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

One of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong. Details leaked on October 20, ahead of the coordinated release, and the PHP project shipped an emergency patch the next day.

The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably. It takes skill and additional knowledge about the target system. Where it matters a lot is appliances, which run identical, often outdated software that an attacker can study in advance. That is the bigger picture. An awful lot of web applications control critical devices in your network. Almost anything is a web application to some extent. That often goes unrecognized, and as a result those applications aren't adequately protected.

Everything is a web application. That is the motto of the SANS course I teach, SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices. Web application security has traditionally been treated as a developer issue, yet anyone protecting a network must understand how web applications work to properly defend them.

Why Appliances Are the Softer Target

On ordinary web servers, address space layout randomization (ASLR) is one of the features that makes exploitation harder. It shuffles where code and data sit in memory, so an exploit can't rely on fixed addresses. VulnCheck's early analysis found the bugs exploitable on ARM64 systems and on x86 systems without ASLR. Few public exploits bypassed ASLR on x86-64, and the one VulnCheck confirmed worked only against a single PHP build. VulnCheck's own exploit chained a memory leak to get code execution with ASLR enabled.

Appliances change that math, not because the protections are missing, but because every device on a given software version runs the same binaries, so an attacker can work out memory offsets in advance. The PAN-OS exploit still had to defeat ASLR, leaking the libphp.so base address through the Set-Cookie header, and SELinux confined the resulting shell. PAN-OS also ships end-of-life PHP versions (8.0.30 and 7.4.33). Israeli security firm Dream, working with Palo Alto Networks on the investigation, found the attacker had obtained PAN-OS firmware, decrypted it, extracted the PHP libraries, and built precise memory profiles for nine software versions. The actor then chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw (Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300) to gain root on 25 systems (24 firewalls and one management server) in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.

Web application security tends to focus on large, cloud-based applications. It's often the little things, the mosquitoes on the internet, that do you in. Appliances run predictable, often outdated software, and they are everywhere.

HTTP Is More Complex Than Your Defenses Assume

HTTP is a very complex protocol with lots of options. To upload a file, a client doesn't have to send it in one piece. It can send the body in chunks without declaring its total length, and, if the server decompresses request bodies, compress it, which makes it difficult for a web server to calculate how much memory it needs to store it. Memory-safety bugs remain common as a result, in web applications and in the web servers running them. In PHP2Shell, a crafted multipart upload pushes PHP past its memory limit while it is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. The bugs […]

title: Researcher Demonstrates Database RCE Exploits Affecting PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle
text:
Researcher Demonstrates Database RCE Exploits Affecting PostgreSQL, MySQL and OracleSwati KhandelwalNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Database Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

Low-privilege database accounts that cannot read a single application table can still be used to run code on the database server itself, a researcher has shown, by reaching memory-corruption bugs in the engine code behind ordinary SQL.

The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login. None has been seen in a real attack.

The work is by Zheng Yu, a researcher at Depthfirst. A database account's SQL permissions control which tables and schemas it can access, the researcher argues, not the memory-unsafe C and C++ code the engine runs to read, plan, and execute a query.

Common grants give an account enough room to reach that code. PostgreSQL's default TEMPORARY privilege, or the right to create temporary tables in MySQL and ClickHouse, allows an account to create objects or send input that triggers a memory bug.

All five flaws now have vendor fixes, four of them with CVEs, but the full attack chains were not reproduced independently, and the research reports no sign that any of them has been used in an attack.

In PostgreSQL, the flaw CVE-2026-116331 allows an account that can create database objects to run code as the operating system user that runs the database.

It was fixed last week in a security advisory, and the CVE record credits the researcher for the report. The researcher's technical analysis shows a plain login role building the objects it needs in its own temporary schema, without touching application data, then turning a type-confusion bug into control of the server.

MySQL has a similar flaw in its query optimizer, CVE-2026-101786, in Server and Cluster versions 26.7.0 to 26.7.1. Oracle's MySQL October advisory rates it as needing high privileges.

The researcher reached code execution on the 26.7.0 image with an account that could only create temporary tables and could not read existing ones, a narrower kind of access than that rating suggests.

Oracle Database is the one case where an attacker needs no account at all, the researcher says. A bug in Oracle Text and a flaw in the GraphQL interface of Oracle REST Data Services, chained against an exposed web endpoint, reach the engine code and run commands before any login.

Oracle patched the Oracle Text bug, CVE-2026-114819, rated 9.9, earlier this week in its November update, and the GraphQL flaw, CVE-2026-91609, in the October update. On their own, the company rates neither as exploitable without a login.

ClickHouse is the fourth target. The researcher reports an integer-overflow write in how it reads a binary row format, reached by a user who sets a single option, format_binary_max_string_size, to zero, and reproduced a shell on version 26.7.5.10.

This one has no CVE. ClickHouse told The Hacker News that the flaw was reported through its bug bounty program and that a fix was released in early September. The open-source fix is in version 26.9 and later, and was backported to the 26.8, 26.7, 26.6 and 26.3 release lines starting with builds 26.8.3.41, 26.7.7.30, 26.6.5.55 and 26.3.32.8.

CISA Warns of 4 Exploited Flaws Linked to Ransomware, Cryptomining, and LLMjacking AttacksRavie LakshmananNov 19, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added four vulnerabilities impacting Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code.
CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in REDCap that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.
CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An unprotected alternate channel vulnerability in LiteLLM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via bytecode rewriting at the /guardrails/test_custom_code URI.
CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in Synology DSM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via unspecified vectors.

"An attacker could exploit this via crafted HTTP requests that access an unintended controller route from a public survey context and supply a crafted file-path or stream parameter during data import processing," CISA said about CVE-2026-90817. "Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash."

The addition of CVE-2026-90436 to the KEV catalog follows reports that the flaw is exploited in conjunction with the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities affecting N-able N-central to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

Rapid7, in its own analysis of the flaw, said it detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment by taking advantage of the fact that the corporate workspace platform uses the Axis library as part of its XML-RPC and SOAP APIs.

"To be vulnerable, the Confluence instance must have the 'Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)' enabled," Atlassian said. "Please note that this setting was turned off by default for new installations starting in Confluence 3.0. This feature was fully removed in Confluence 10.0."

In the activity documented by Rapid7, threat actors are said to have weaponized the flaw to run shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains, followed by enumerating the compromised environment. The incident was flagged on November 13, 2026.

"Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys," Rapid7 said.

"The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives."

In addition, the attackers have been found to map various internal services, use a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, and attempt to carry out a Kerberos-based credential harvesting technique called AS-REP Roasting.

Although these efforts were unsuccessful, the threat actor managed to acquire a service account credential and queried a production cloud data warehouse. About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the […]

Vulnerability Details
This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP UpdateFirmware requests. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a write past the end of an allocated buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device.

Since 04/14/26, ZDI has made multiple attempts to contact United Chargers to establish a vendor disclosure channel for the vulnerabilities identified in the Grizzl-E Smart 40A during Pwn2Own Automotive 2026. Despite these repeated efforts, both before and after the contest, the vendor has not responded to any communication.

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

CVE-2026-114938 - OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Intrinsic Out-of-Bounds Write Issue

Bulletin ID: 2026-189-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/18/2026 19:00 PM PST
Last Updated Date: 11/19/2026 14:00 PM PST

Summary:

AWS is aware of CVE-2026-114938, a memory issue in the Base64 decoder intrinsic of OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI. Affected processors include Intel Ice Lake and later and AMD Zen 4 and later. Under specific conditions, a remote, unauthenticated third party can send crafted Base64 input to an application that decodes untrusted data. This results in an out-of-bounds memory write.

Java workloads running natively on AWS Graviton processors are not affected. We have no evidence that this issue has been leveraged at this time.

We will update this bulletin as more information becomes available.

Current Mitigation Status:

Amazon Corretto: Amazon Corretto versions 27.0.1.1.4, 25.0.5.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 17.0.21.1.2 and updated OpenJDK packages for Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 are available. Customers running Java workloads on affected x86-64 instances should update to these versions. Customers who can't update right away can set the JVM option -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as an interim mitigation.

Amazon Linux: Amazon Corretto packages that resolve CVE-2026-114938 are available for Amazon Linux 2, Amazon Linux 2023 and the Amazon Linux 2027 Preview. Amazon Linux rates this issue Important (CVSS v3 8.8). Customers running Amazon Corretto 17 or later on Amazon Linux should update each installed Corretto package and restart their Java applications. No reboot is needed.

Bulletin ID: 2026-190-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/19/2026 10:00 AM PST

Summary:

AWS is aware of security releases that the PHP Foundation published on November 19, 2026. PHP versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13 address 17 issues across the PHP 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5 branches. The issues are in the following components:

The PHP engine
PHP-FPM and the PHP CGI binary
The SOAP, Phar, session, DOM, and date extensions
The HTTP and FTP stream wrappers
The PHP 8.5 RFC 3986 URI implementation

Under specific conditions, some of these issues could allow a remote, unauthenticated third party to cause a PHP process to stop responding, access process memory, or run code in the context of the affected PHP process.

PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life and won't receive these fixes. Some of these issues affect those releases, including CVE-2026-129289. If you run PHP 8.1 or earlier, we recommend that you move to a supported PHP branch.

Patching the affected software remains the only complete fix and should be the first priority. We will update this bulletin as more information becomes available.

Current Mitigation Status:

Amazon Linux: Updated PHP packages that address the CVEs in this bulletin are available for Amazon Linux 2023 in all AWS Regions. Updated packages for Amazon Linux 2 and the Amazon Linux 2027 Preview are being released, and we will update this bulletin when they are available. Amazon Linux 2023: php8.2-8.2.36-1.amzn2023.0.1 (ALAS2023-2026-3504), php8.3-8.3.37-1.amzn2023.0.1 (ALAS2023-2026-3505), php8.4-8.4.28-1.amzn2023.0.1 (ALAS2023-2026-3507), php8.5-8.5.13-1.amzn2023.0.1 (ALAS2023-2026-3506) To update Amazon Linux 2023, run the command for the PHP version you have installed: sudo dnf upgrade --releasever=latest php8.2-8.2.36-1.amzn2023.0.1 sudo dnf upgrade --releasever=latest php8.3-8.3.37-1.amzn2023.0.1 sudo dnf upgrade --releasever=latest php8.4-8.4.28-1.amzn2023.0.1 sudo dnf upgrade --releasever=latest php8.5-8.5.13-1.amzn2023.0.1 If you lock Amazon Linux 2023 to a release version, use release 2023.12.20261119.0 or later. After updating, restart the services that run PHP, such as php-fpm or httpd (for example, sudo systemctl restart php-fpm). A reboot is not required. CVE-2026-132607 - GCM authentication tag length downgrade in Amazon S3 Encryption Client for PHP

Bulletin ID: 2026-191-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/19/2026 13:00 PM PST

Description:

Amazon S3 Encryption Client for PHP is a client-side encryption library, included in the AWS SDK for PHP, that encrypts and decrypts objects stored in Amazon S3.

We identified CVE-2026-132607, an issue in the decryption component of Amazon S3 Encryption Client for PHP in the AWS SDK for PHP. The client did not verify the length of the AES-GCM authentication tag recorded in an object's metadata. A user with read and write access to an encrypted object, who knows or can guess its plaintext, might craft a ciphertext that decrypts to plaintext of their choice of the same length. This requires repeated writes to the object. The issue does not disclose the plaintext or the encryption key.

Impacted versions: >= 3.148.0 AND <= 3.383.0

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in AWS SDK for PHP version 3.383.1. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

There are no workarounds for this issue. Customers must upgrade to AWS SDK for PHP version 3.383.1 or later.

References:

CVE-2026-132607
GHSA-9c62-hqw2-gj46

Issue with nginx HTTP/2 Implementation

Bulletin ID: 2026-192-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/19/2026 15:00 PM PST

Summary:

AWS is aware of the nginx issues published on November 18, 2026 (CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-113425, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-118899). These issues have been addressed in nginx version 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline). We recommend upgrading to the latest version. We are actively deploying mitigations worldwide to address these issues.

Because these issues can be leveraged at the HTTP/2 protocol layer before a complete HTTP request is formed, AWS WAF managed and custom rules cannot effectively detect or block them.

Current Mitigation Status:

Amazon Linux customers: Patched nginx packages are available for Amazon Linux 2, Amazon Linux 2023, and Amazon Linux 2027. Update using your standard package manager:

# Amazon Linux 2 / Amazon Linux 2023 / Amazon Linux 2027
sudo yum update nginx

Amazon Linux Security Advisories (ALAS) have been published for all five CVEs:

https://explore.alas.aws.amazon.com/CVE-2026-123007.html
https://explore.alas.aws.amazon.com/CVE-2026-123633.html
https://explore.alas.aws.amazon.com/CVE-2026-123634.html
https://explore.alas.aws.amazon.com/CVE-2026-121810.html
https://explore.alas.aws.amazon.com/CVE-2026-113425.html

AWS Elastic Beanstalk customers: The fix has been released and is available. Only environments where customers have enabled HTTP/2 on their own nginx listener are affected. The default configuration does not enable HTTP/2. Until you can apply the patch, disabling HTTP/2 on custom listeners mitigates the two Critical HTTP/2 issues.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

CVE-2026-132825 and related issues – Ruby regular expression engine and string case conversion

Bulletin ID: 2026-193-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/19/2026 15:05 PM PST
Last Updated Date: 11/19/2026 15:50 PM PST

Description:

On November 18, 2026, the Ruby maintainers published fixes for seven issues in CRuby's regular expression engine and string case conversion, including CVE-2026-132825. These issues affect Ruby versions before 4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14 and could allow remote code execution in some configurations.

These issues are memory-safety issues in Ruby's regular expression engine and in string case conversion on certain non-UTF-8 encodings. When an application processes third party-controlled input through these code paths, a remote, unauthenticated actor might be able to crash the process, read memory, or run arbitrary code. Applications built on Rack, including Rails and Sinatra, might be reachable through default request handling.

Affected versions:

Ruby before 4.0.10, before 3.4.13, and before 3.3.14. Ruby 3.2 and earlier versions are end of life and will not receive upstream fixes.

Current Mitigation Status:

AWS Elastic Beanstalk released updated Ruby platforms on Amazon Linux 2023 (platform version 4.15.4) on 2026-11-19. Updates include Ruby 3.3 to 3.3.14, Ruby 3.4 to 3.4.13, and Ruby 4.0 to 4.0.10. Customers using Elastic Beanstalk Ruby platforms should update their environments to platform version 4.15.4, either through managed platform updates or by updating the environment.

Amazon Linux is releasing updated Ruby packages that address these issues, targeted for 2026-11-20. The updates cover the ruby3.2, ruby3.4, and ruby4.0 packages on Amazon Linux 2023 and the ruby3.4 package on Amazon Linux 2027. Customers should apply them when they appear in the Amazon Linux Security Center. The core Ruby 2.0.0 package on Amazon Linux 2 is not affected,

We are investigating impact on AWS services, including managed Ruby runtimes and platforms. We will update this bulletin with service-specific status and any required customer actions as more information becomes available.

Interim step for customers who cannot update immediately:

There are no workarounds that fully mitigate these issues. Customers who cannot update immediately should limit susceptibility of internet-facing Ruby applications and avoid processing untrusted input in non-UTF-8 encodings where possible.

Customers who manage their own Ruby installations should upgrade to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14 or later. Customers on Ruby 3.2 or earlier should upgrade to a supported Ruby version. Customers using Amazon Linux should apply the updated packages listed in the Amazon Linux Security Center when available.

If you use AWS WAF, we plan to release version 1.29 of the AWS Managed Rules Known Bad Inputs rule group by November 19 at 7:30 PM PST.
