title: 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable
text:
30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable

November 19, 2026

Abstract

We give an exposition for a principle of gatekeeper asymmetry doom in information security, which states that “If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.” We list a variety of examples where one can see this principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and our own ‘PuzzleMask’ research for bypassing external AI guardrails, as well as a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem also exemplifies this same principle. We conclude with a recommendation that “doomed” attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap be narrowed down as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or making use of its existing power more comprehensively. We note that frontier LLMs (with scaffolding, extended reasoning, code execution in the chain of thought, and so on) have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing “doom” gaps, though ultimately, they themselves are still subject to this principle.

Introduction

In the same spirit of Moxie Marlinspike’s Cryptographic Doom Principle [1], the Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom principle states that:

If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.

By the mention of ‘leveraging a hard problem’ we mean to exclude e.g. signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still, at least in a certain theoretical world, determine whether the binary is malicious or not. The principle might be phrased more glibly as “every quick sanity check involves either cryptography or a silent prayer.”

From now on, rather than writing out “gatekeeper asymmetry doom” every time, we will simply refer to “doom” for short. We’ll start with examples that are more on the “warm-up” side and gradually go from those to less intuitive ones where the application of the principle is more surprising.

Examples

Hash Comparison

A good warm-up example to start with is the one burned into the psyche of every infosec practitioner in some fundamental post-traumatic sense.

At some point during the 1990s, the silent thought must have come to someone in the industry that malware was solved. You could collect all the hashes of malicious binaries in a large database and then a gatekeeper, called in this case an “antivirus,” would check each executed binary against the known list of ‘bad’ hashes. Of course, new threats would emerge periodically, and the list would have to be updated, but this was a caveat – not a dealbreaker.

The gap between the gatekeeper’s power and the target’s power here was truly huge. The target in this case is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary, and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. The procedure effectively strips all other file data and precludes it from consideration, and the threat actors’ counter was infamous and trivial: for each compiled binary, randomize the value of some non-load-bearing byte. This is more a precursor to Gatekeeper Asymmetry than the proper thing itself: what’s doing the work in motivating hash comparisons is less a notion that the file has been ‘analyzed’ in some way, and more a bundle of implicit assumptions regarding where, how and when malicious binaries come into being. Still, there is a straight line connecting the initial concept of hash comparison and the rest of the fraught journey of attempting to classify binaries by static analysis alone.

Pattern Matching

Since the days of the simple hash comparison, the gatekeeping models for static analysis have grown more complex and powerful. […]

title: From posture to root cause: Investigate OpenShift compliance with Elastic Agent Builder
text: BlogFrom posture to root cause: Investigate OpenShift compliance with Elastic Agent BuilderWhen an OpenShift compliance control fails, Elastic Agent Builder traces the root cause, from Compliance Operator scans centralized in Elasticsearch and CEL checks for the rules the scanner marks manual.November 19, 2026Anand VyasAI & AutomationCloud SecurityIntegrations & ToolsJump to Share A single Elastic Agent on each cluster polls OpenShift Compliance Operator APIs every 60 seconds. An Elastic Agent Builder agent on top of that data can tell you what change failed the compliance control. Every scan and check result lands in Elasticsearch, as do the remediations, so the agent answers questions (like, Which clusters failed checks this week? Why did a control start failing, and when?) in plain English.  The rules that the scanner marks as manual get evaluated with Common Expression Language (CEL) custom rules, and a scheduled workflow in Elastic Workflows annotates the result back to the manual rule in the cluster. Rescans and remediation patches run through those same workflows and pause for your approval. Everything in this post is on GitHub, including the integration package and workflows, along with the manifests.The Compliance Operator scans each OpenShift cluster against configured profiles covering the CIS Benchmarks, National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53 moderate (the basis for Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program [FedRAMP] authorization), the Australian Essential Eight and more, and then stores the results on that cluster. For one cluster, that’s fine, but across a fleet, nobody has a single view. A rule that passed last week starts failing after a deployment, and a scheduled scan silently fails to trigger. But the only way to find out is to log in and run oc get compliancecheckresult cluster by cluster.Why OpenShift compliance is hard to track across a fleetScan results stored on each clusterThe Compliance Operator runs scans on each OpenShift cluster and stores the results locally. This approach works across a few clusters, but as the fleet grows, it becomes difficult for OpenShift administrators to maintain visibility across each cluster.A compliance rule that had previously passed might start to fail after a new workload deployment or a cluster upgrade. Similarly, a scheduled scan can fail to trigger, due to unresolved dependencies. Without a central view of compliance scan status and results, these failures go unnoticed until an OpenShift administrator logs in to the cluster and manually checks, using commands such as oc get compliancecheckresult and oc get compliancescan.In this blog post, we explore how this challenge can be addressed by ingesting OpenShift compliance data into Elasticsearch, giving platform and security teams a unified way to track compliance posture and investigate drift across the fleet.Manual compliance rules tracked outside the clusterNot all compliance rules are automated, so they need a manual assessment. Platform teams usually track these rules and their status in shared spreadsheets or Confluence pages. Those trackers sit apart from the scan results, and someone has to update and reconcile them with each cluster’s findings.Organizational controls add another layer. A team may exclude certain controls from specific clusters because of internal requirements or operational needs. Without a central record, it’s hard to determine which controls apply to which cluster and why an exception exists, and that’s exactly what an auditor will ask. With scan results spread across clusters, security teams have to find their own way to aggregate the data before they can build a report. Auditors can ask for reports at regular intervals, so this aggregation repeats every cycle. Each report draws on scan output and manual rule status, along with documented exceptions that live in different places. Pulling all of that together can leave gaps.Centralizing OpenShift compliance […]

title: NGINX2Root: Path to code execution and root compromise
text:
November 19, 2026

|

Security intelligence

NGINX2Root: Path to code execution and root compromise

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

F5 fixed 10 vulnerabilities in NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus, including five critical flaws disclosed as part of the NGINX2Root research that may lead to code execution under specific conditions.

Researchers demonstrated code execution against affected NGINX deployments, and public proof-of-concept code for CVE-2026-123007 was released on November 18, 2026.

Internet-facing NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled are the most relevant systems to review. This includes reverse proxies, Kubernetes ingress controllers, load balancers, and application gateways that sit in front of websites, applications, and APIs.

Threat summary
On November 18, 2026, F5 released an out-of-band security update fixing 10 vulnerabilities in NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus.
Five of those form “NGINX2Root,” the name Xint gave to a set of flaws that demonstrated paths from internet-accessible NGINX services to code execution. In some cases they also led to root access on the underlying host, when combined with a separate, unpatched Linux kernel vulnerability.
Researchers from Rapid7, Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, and Metnir independently reported overlapping findings.
The other five vulnerabilities are configuration-dependent issues affecting specific NGINX features. Their reported impact includes denial-of-service, client certificate bypass, access to internal resources, and, in one uncommon configuration, a buffer overflow with theoretical code execution. They are rated medium to high severity, with CVSS v4 scores from 6.3 to 8.7.
NGINX2Root
NGINX is one of the most widely deployed web servers and reverse proxies in enterprise environments. It is also commonly embedded in Kubernetes ingress controllers, container images, application gateways, commercial software, and security appliances, which can make affected deployments hard to identify.
The NGINX2Root research covers five vulnerabilities across four components:

HTTP/2: CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633

HTTP/3: CVE-2026-121810

DNS resolver: CVE-2026-123634

Mail proxy: CVE-2026-113425

The HTTP/2 vulnerabilities received the most attention because they are subject to a public exploit code. These vulnerabilities affect NGINX deployments that expose HTTP/2 services to untrusted networks.
CVE-2026-123007 applies to systems with HTTP/2 enabled, while CVE-2026-123633 only affects deployments that use NGINX as a reverse proxy under specific connection-management conditions.
F5 describes both vulnerabilities as memory corruption flaws that can cause worker process crashes and, under certain circumstances, may lead to remote code execution.
Rapid7 published a proof-of-concept (PoC) code repository containing a worker-process crash trigger and a full exploit that executed commands against NGINX 1.31.8 running in a Docker container. The repository notes state the exploit is suitable only against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine.
Other repositories claiming to exploit CVE-2026-123007 have appeared on GitHub, and reports of fake exploits have been circulating.
The full exploit depends on conditions beyond the presence of a vulnerable server:

Approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic over a single connection, delivered within NGINX's default one-hour connection lifetime
Direct HTTP/2 access to the target server
An exploit calibrated for the target's exact NGINX build and C library
A target with little other traffic, since concurrent requests can cause the attempt to fail
An x86-64 processor with AVX2 or AVX-512; the attack fails against the older SSE memory-copy routine, but nearly all current server processors support AVX2

The exploit defeats Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on its own by leaking memory addresses through the same flaw, so ASLR-enabled targets are not protected.

title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere
text:
Threat IntelligenceARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphereNovember 19, 2026Google Threat Intelligence Group Mandiant Mandiant ServicesStop attacks, reduce risk, and advance your security.Contact Mandiant Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram

Introduction 
On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05. We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. 
On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. 
ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account.
ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat. 
Threat Detail 
Moving laterally from the Remote SupportRemote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft.Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of eventsMove Laterally
Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui. The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an […]

title: Regional Insights: 2027 State of Threat Intelligence
text:
PUBLISHED ON 19 NOV 2026

Conor Hoy, Product Marketing

Recorded Future’s 2027 State of Threat Intelligence report surveyed 768 security professionals worldwide on how they use threat intelligence today, how they apply AI to it, and where they plan to invest. The report presents the global findings. The regional executive summaries in this blog cover insights from the same survey, breaking data down by global region into dedicated briefs covering the specific conclusions for cybersecurity leaders in North America, EMEA, APJ, and LATAM. Start with your region to see how your peers are approaching threat intelligence, and read the others for a wider view.North America (United States and Canada)In North America, threat intelligence now informs decisions well beyond the security organization. Five teams consume it on average, and 85% of organizations surveyed have teams outside core security using it, including risk management (54%), fraud prevention (44%), and risk and compliance (44%). With intelligence supporting this many teams, 81% plan to invest more in the next 12 months. The challenge is getting the right intelligence to each of those teams in a form they can act on.Doing that depends on how well intelligence comes together, and this is an ongoing effort for many programs. Most surveyed organizations (63%) draw on four or more intelligence vendors. Only 21% combine that external intelligence with their own internal telemetry in a single platform, where analysts can see which threats apply to their environment. Consolidation plans reflect this. Of the 76% planning to consolidate, the largest share are doing it to improve correlation across signals (40%), compared with only 8% who cite cost.Moving intelligence from those sources to risk owners is also largely manual. 54% put intelligence into action manually across tools and processes. Among organizations sharing intelligence outside security, 38% rely on ad hoc messages or scheduled reports. Manual handoffs make it harder to see what risk owners did with the intelligence and whether it worked. While 98% measure program value, 28% track whether triggered actions were effective. Only 22% report closed-loop operationalization, where stakeholders act on intelligence, the results are validated, and those results inform the program’s priorities and collection.AI is already part of this work for nearly all respondents (98%), and 60% use agents that take actions inside their intelligence tools. Leaders become more cautious as the stakes rise: comfort with letting AI act falls from 71% for summarization to 56% for enforcement actions. The leading barriers are lack of auditability (40%) and unproven accuracy (31%). 73% say intelligence regularly feeds their AI and automation systems or is a core input to them. That makes the quality and correlation of their intelligence a factor in how far they can trust AI to act.Risk owners can come from procurement, legal, fraud, corporate security, or communications. Threat intelligence innovation means getting the intelligence to the right person to make decisions and take action based on that intelligence.
Rich LaTulip
North America Field CISO at Recorded Future
This summary draws on responses from 347 North American security professionals. They were part of a global survey of 768 that asked how organizations use threat intelligence, apply AI to it, and plan future investments.The full report covers how intelligence is expanding across the business, what full visibility requires, and what stands between teams and proven impact.

Europe, Middle East, and Africa (EMEA)Across EMEA, threat intelligence now informs decisions well beyond the security organization, and leaders plan to extend it further. 86% of organizations surveyed have teams outside core security using it, and 35% name expanding intelligence to more teams as a top priority for the next two years. Pierluigi Paganini

November 19, 2026
The researcher Chaotic Eclipse released FastUnlock, a new Windows zero-day vulnerability exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen.

Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as INFINITE NIGHTMARE, MSNightmare and Nightmare-Eclipse, released a new Windows zero-day vulnerability, dubbed FastUnlock, exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen.

According to the researcher, exploiting it can bypass BitLocker encryption and allow code execution under the lock screen’s WsiAccount. He claims he breached a fully encrypted Windows 11 26H2 system in just five minutes, even with the November security updates installed.

“It took a total of 5 minutes from finding this to breaching a fully encrypted bitlocker machine with Windows 11 26H2 November Patch installed, an issue caused by total negligence from Microsoft’s side… The vulnerability seems to be extremely consistent in every machine I tested it in, in other words, if you know how to control narrator in the background properly or just press the correct combination of buttons, you will get code execution in the target machine as well.” reads the advisory published by the researcher.

The attack requires physical access to the computer and at least one user account linked to an online account. The researcher says the flaw undermines BitLocker’s protection, which should prevent access to encrypted data even if an attacker has physical access to the device.

He explains that Microsoft introduced the issue while redesigning Narrator, failing to prevent its new interface from running in the lock screen account context. Unlike earlier lock screen bypass flaws, this one is reportedly easier to exploit. The attack can be triggered through the “I forgot my PIN” or password option.

A cyberattack has disrupted internal European Commission systems for more than ten days, hitting payroll, leave requests and medical reimbursements. Sysper, the HR platform for payslips, timesheets and leave, crashed briefly again on 18 November after access had been restored earlier in the week. MyPMO, the medical reimbursement system, came back online around the same time. Some staff still complained the internal communication said little, and an IT reply about the Sysper problem cited a general technical issue without mentioning an attack.

Pierluigi Paganini

PHP will patch critical security flaws across supported versions, including a session handling bug that could allow remote code execution.

The PHP development team announced a new security release scheduled for November 19, warning that the updates will address vulnerabilities across all supported versions of the widely used server-side programming language. The highest severity rating is CRITICAL, although the project says the affected issues require unusual configurations or non-default setups.

The announcement places the release within PHP’s regular four-week update cycle.

One vulnerability expected to be addressed is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw involving PHP session handling.

nginx2root exposes five critical nginx flaws and a Linux kernel bug that can lead to remote code execution and root access.

Xint Research has disclosed nginx2root, five distinct nginx vulnerabilities plus one Linux kernel bug, each with a proven exploit. The worst of the five, now tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an unauthenticated attacker run code remotely, and chaining it with the kernel bug reaches root on the host.

“This issue affects NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source configurations that use HTTP/2. When NGINX processes undisclosed traffic, the flow control window can exceed the allowed threshold, potentially resulting in a heap buffer overflow typically followed by an NGINX worker segmentation fault. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR. (CVE-2026-123007)” reads the advisory. “An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to crash the NGINX worker process, corrupt its memory, or potentially execute code remotely. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.”

Affected nginx versions run from 1.9.5 to 1.31.8, and the fix landed in 1.31.9. According to Zakir Durumeric, Co-Founder and CEO Censys, nearly 10M Internet services are running versions of Nginx vulnerable to the NGINX2Root CVEs.

The bug sits in nginx’s HTTP/2 flow control, and it’s been there since nginx added HTTP/2 in 2015, eleven years ago. An attacker corrupts memory in an nginx worker, leaks memory addresses, and overwrites a pointer to a cleanup function that fires when a connection closes.

At one point during the breach, 41 PowerShell modules ran under a webshell on an Internet Information Services (IIS) server in three minutes and twelve seconds, with a new module starting every few seconds. The modules tested credentials, a reused bearer token and API keys against the exchange's own investment API and the gateway of a securities depository.The toolkit is one of the clearest examples of suspected machine-written attack tooling that we have seen to date. Every module shared the same scaffold, and a Domain Name System (DNS) exfiltration loop was copied byte for byte into all 41 scripts, where a programmer would normally write it once as a shared function. Each module sent its output as hex-encoded DNS lookups to a public out-of-band testing service, a rarely seen technique. The results went to a collector that we cannot see, so we do not know whether any of the credentials or keys worked.The earliest evidence of malicious activity on the server dated from April 2026, but the attackers may have been present for longer. Six persistence implants were installed on the server. We attribute the implants to the China-linked espionage group Witchetty (aka LookingFrog) with high confidence, but we have not attributed the activity described below to any group. It could be Witchetty using new tooling, a second and more capable operator using the same access, or an unrelated actor who has compromised the same server. The target suggests the attack was financially motivated. title: CVE-2026-123007: Critical NGINX2Root HTTP/2 Flaw Enables Remote Code Execution
text:
En

CVEs

November 19, 2026
8 min read

F5 has released emergency security updates addressing CVE-2026-123007, a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in NGINX that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code on vulnerable web servers. Dubbed NGINX2Root, the flaw resides in NGINX’s HTTP/2 flow-control implementation and has been present in the codebase for more than a decade.

The vulnerability carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2. An attacker who can reach an HTTP/2-enabled NGINX listener can manipulate flow-control state until an invalid response length causes out-of-bounds memory access. Depending on the target environment, exploitation can crash an NGINX worker, disclose memory, corrupt process memory, or enable arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the worker process.

NGINX Open Source releases from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 are vulnerable. F5 released fixed versions 1.30.7 for the stable branch and 1.31.9 for mainline on November 18, 2026. NGINX Plus is also affected across multiple 37.x and older supported branches.

The flaw is particularly concerning because authentication is not required. Xint researchers demonstrated remote command execution through a reachable HTTP/2 service, while Rapid7 independently developed an unauthenticated RCE exploit against NGINX 1.31.8. However, obtaining root privileges on the underlying operating system requires a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability or another post-exploitation technique.

Security teams can also use Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into detection logic, generate hunting queries, refine existing rules, and adapt behavioral detections to their organization’s telemetry.

Detect CVE-2026-123007 by combining HTTP/2 network telemetry with NGINX worker behavior, crash events, and host-level process activity. Suspicious HTTP/2 traffic followed by worker segmentation faults, abnormal child processes, shell execution, or unexpected outbound connections from NGINX should receive immediate investigation.

CVE-2026-123007 analysis

CVE-2026-123007 affects NGINX deployments using HTTP/2. The vulnerability originates in the way NGINX manages HTTP/2 flow-control windows, which determine how much DATA a server can transmit to a client across individual streams and the overall connection.

HTTP/2 clients can increase available flow-control credit using WINDOW_UPDATE frames. NGINX maintains separate counters for individual streams and the connection itself. The protocol limits these flow-control windows to 2^31-1 bytes, but the vulnerable implementation can be manipulated into exceeding the permitted connection-window threshold.

Rapid7’s analysis describes a multi-stage condition in which an attacker keeps response data queued, manipulates stream and connection credits, and forces selected streams to close. Cleanup of those streams can restore reserved credit to the connection counter, pushing it above the HTTP/2 maximum. A subsequent unsigned subtraction can then underflow, allowing additional WINDOW_UPDATE frames to drive the counter to an invalid value.

Eventually, NGINX interprets the excessive unsigned connection window as a negative signed response length. During buffered output processing, that value can be converted into an extremely large unsigned length passed to memory-copy operations, resulting in out-of-bounds reads and writes in the NGINX worker’s heap.

The immediate result is often a worker segmentation fault. Under favorable memory-layout conditions, however, researchers demonstrated that the corruption can be converted into controlled memory disclosure and modification. This can […]

title: CVE-2026-123633: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Use-After-Free Flaw Enables RCE
text:
En

CVEs

November 19, 2026
9 min read

A newly disclosed vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-123633 exposes certain NGINX reverse-proxy deployments to unauthenticated denial-of-service attacks and potentially remote code execution. The flaw is a use-after-free condition in NGINX’s HTTP/2 processing that can be triggered when the server proxies client requests to an upstream backend while a worker is running low on available connections.

The vulnerability was disclosed alongside CVE-2026-123007 as part of a broader set of security flaws patched by the NGINX team on November 18, 2026. F5 assigns CVE-2026-123633 a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, Critical, while its CVSS v3.1 score is 8.1, High because exploitation requires a particular server state and configuration.

Unlike CVE-2026-123007, which can affect HTTP/2-enabled NGINX instances serving ordinary static content, CVE-2026-123633 specifically targets reverse-proxy processing. An exposed server must have HTTP/2 enabled, forward requests to a backend server, and reach a state where available worker_connections are running low.

Successful exploitation can crash NGINX worker processes or corrupt memory. Wiz researchers demonstrated that the vulnerability can be developed into unauthenticated remote code execution and confirmed an ASLR bypass in laboratory environments. Code execution occurs with the privileges of the NGINX worker process rather than automatically granting root access to the host.

Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize vulnerability intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Contact Sales

Detect CVE-2026-123633 by correlating abnormal HTTP/2 traffic and connection exhaustion with NGINX worker crashes, suspicious process execution, and unexpected network connections originating from NGINX processes. Because exploitation occurs in the web-server process itself, combining network and endpoint telemetry provides substantially stronger visibility than relying on static indicators alone.

CVE-2026-123633 analysis

CVE-2026-123633 affects NGINX Open Source versions beginning with 1.19.7 through 1.31.8 when HTTP/2 is enabled and requests are proxied to an upstream backend. NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 contain the fix. NGINX Plus is also affected, with fixes for this specific vulnerability introduced in 37.0.7.1 and 37.2.0.1.

The underlying weakness is a use-after-free condition in NGINX’s HTTP/2 connection management. NGINX keeps a list of connections marked as reusable so it can close them when additional connection slots are required. A connection should only remain on that list when it has no active request being processed.

Researchers found that an attacker can initially send only part of an HTTP/2 HEADERS frame. Because no active stream has yet been created, NGINX marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the remainder of the frame.

After the attacker sends the remaining portion, NGINX creates an HTTP/2 request stream and begins processing the request. However, the connection can incorrectly remain marked as reusable even though it is now actively handling a request. This creates the precondition for the memory-safety flaw.

The attacker then causes the request to be forwarded to an upstream application server. Establishing that backend connection requires NGINX to obtain another connection slot. When the worker approaches its configured worker_connections limit, NGINX can invoke its connection-draining logic to free capacity.

title: CVE-2026-129448: Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw Exploited in the Wild
text:
Apache has disclosed a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting Apache Roller, an open-source Java-based blogging and content management platform. Tracked as CVE-2026-129448, the flaw enables an unauthenticated remote attacker to send malicious data to Roller’s XML-RPC endpoint and trigger deserialization before authentication checks occur. Apache has confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited in real-world attacks.

The vulnerability carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical, with low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction. Successful exploitation can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the context of the application server, potentially providing control over the Roller deployment and access to data, credentials, or other resources available to the compromised Java process.

The issue affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. It is the same underlying security weakness as CVE-2026-82384, which was disclosed in September 2026 and specifically documented Apache Roller 6.1.5 as vulnerable. Taken together, the two CVE records show that installations from Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.5 should be treated as vulnerable and upgraded to 6.1.6 or later.

The risk is heightened by the fact that disabling XML-RPC through the Roller administration interface alone does not prevent exploitation on vulnerable releases. The affected endpoint can deserialize attacker-controlled request content before the application checks whether XML-RPC functionality has been disabled.

Security teams can also use Prime Architect to turn emerging vulnerability intelligence into hunting queries, refine detection rules, and adapt behavioral detection logic to the telemetry available across their infrastructure.

Contact Sales

Detect CVE-2026-129448 by monitoring requests to Roller’s /roller-services/xmlrpc endpoint and correlating suspicious XML-RPC traffic with unexpected Java process behavior, shell execution, file creation, outbound connections, or application-server anomalies.

CVE-2026-129448 analysis

CVE-2026-129448 affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. Apache describes the issue as Deserialization of Untrusted Data, mapped to CWE-502, in Roller’s XML-RPC functionality. The endpoint accepts non-standard vendor extension types and processes them before authenticating the client.

Apache Roller exposes an XML-RPC servlet at:

/roller-services/xmlrpc

The XML-RPC implementation historically allowed vendor-specific extension types in addition to standard XML-RPC values. Roller itself does not require those extension types, but older configurations enabled them at the servlet level.

The critical security issue is the order in which incoming requests are processed. The XML-RPC parser accepts and deserializes extension-type values while parsing the request body. Authentication and feature-state checks happen later. As a result, an unauthenticated attacker can cause attacker-controlled serialized data to reach Java deserialization logic before Roller has established whether the request should be permitted.

This ordering effectively places a dangerous deserialization primitive on a remotely reachable endpoint. In vulnerable deployments, an attacker does not need a valid Roller account, administrator credentials, or user interaction to reach the affected code path.

text:
Court Tells Cops That The 4th Amendment Doesn’t Cover AI-Generated ‘Probable Cause’

Legal Issues

from the remember-that-time-robocop-shot-the-Constitution-in-the-dick dept

Thu, Nov 19th 2026 01:19pm -

Tim Cushing

I don’t know where this decision will take us, but its implications reach much further than the single case it covers. AI is pretty much everywhere, and if a court says an algorithm can’t make probable cause determinations, it affects/infects everything from facial recognition tech to predictive policing software to Axon adding AI shovelware to its omnipresent body cameras under the (correct) assumption cops don’t like writing reports.
In this case, Alain Osorio was arrested for allegedly passing a bad check at local bank. The only pictures of the suspect came from the bank’s CCTV footage. This was handed over to Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence (KY) Police Department.
The detective decided to run a screenshot of the suspect’s face (derived from the CCTV footage) through the PD’s facial recognition program. The decision [PDF] doesn’t specify which facial recognition program was used, but given that the match was made using photos found on Facebook, it suggests Clearview AI might have been involved, given its scraping of hundreds of billions of images from the open web since its inception.
Not that it did anything useful in terms of actual detective work. Nor did it do anything remotely constitutional, not when the operative word in “probable cause” is “probable.”

Relying solely on the AI identification, Detective Kilmer concluded that the match was accurate. [Id. at 4–5]. The Facebook profile belonged to an individual known as “Yony Smith Npoles Charon,” and for an unknown reason, Detective Kilmer concluded that “Yony” was actually Alain Vizcay Osorio—the man in the booking photo.

The court says “for an unknown reason.” I can make an educated guess, however. Passing a bad check is the sort of crime most cops won’t really dig into. Detective Kilmer was handed the case and did the bare minimum: he ran an AI-assisted search. He didn’t actually do anything that resembled actual detective work. But he still felt his 30 seconds of non-existent effort were enough to support a criminal complaint and the issuance of an arrest warrant.
Osorio — who lived in Nebraska — was arrested and extradited to Kentucky to face criminal charges. He was released on bond the day after his arrest (January 24, 2025). He was then indicted by a grand jury in March 2025 and arraigned roughly two months later. Again, Osorio pleaded not guilty. At that point, the state’s attorney’s office dismissed the charges after Osorio provided proof he had been working in Nebraska at the time the bad check was being passed by (the presumably still at-large) suspect captured by the bank’s security camera.
The only thing the AI used by the detective seemed to be capable of doing was reinforcing the investigator’s “all Black people look the same” prejudices. (To be clear, I don’t specifically know if this detective has these prejudices, but the chain of events in this case certainly support an assumption of this person’s assumptions, if you catch my drift.)

The individuals in the security footage and the Facebook profile image do not resemble the booking photo of Osorio. [Id. at 6–7]. Based on the booking photo, the only thing Osorio has in common with the suspect is that he is a black male with facial hair. [Dkt. 3-1 at 2–3]. Based on the photographs, it appears that Osorio has a different head shape, different haircut, different facial features, and different complexion.

Detective Kilmer told the court (via his affidavit) that he had used “investigative tools” to “match” Osario to the suspect. In reality, the court says, Kilmer only used a single tool and rolled with its obviously faulty conclusions despite Florence PD policy specifically stating facial recognition AI alone is not enough to “establish probable cause.”

Poland's Cyber Command Says US Tipped It to Russian Attacks
Most NATO Aid to Ukraine Travels Through Poland

Shaun Waterman •
November 19, 2026

A Polish military convoy outside Warsaw in a photo dated Aug. 15, 2026. (Image: Grand Warszawski/Shutterstock)

Polish authorities were first tipped off about Russian cyber threats to their national transportation and power systems by the United States, the head of Poland's Cyber Command told the Billington Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity Summit in San Antonio, Texas this week.See Also: OnDemand | How Okta and CrowdStrike Share Signals to Enforce Protection Against Cross-Domain Attacks
Elements of U.S. Cyber Command also worked with their Polish counterparts to hunt Russian hackers on Polish networks. "It actually started with you guys, with the aid from U.S. institutions," Maj. Gen Mariusz Chmielewski said at a fireside chat Tuesday, where he gave new details about the context and setting of a large-scale, but ultimately by Russian hackers to shut down parts of Poland's power grid just after Christmas last year, when the country was gripped by a fierce winter freeze and the temperature was 5-10 degrees Fahrenheit.
Technical elements of the attack were disclosed in extraordinary detail earlier this year by CERT-PL, the country's national Cyber Emergency Response Team.
After the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, explained Chmielewski, Poland became the almost exclusive route by which military aid from the North Atlantic alliance could reach Ukraine.
"At least 90% of that [aid] goes through Poland" arriving by sea or air and taken by road or rail to Ukraine, he said, in rare comments from Poland's top cyber warrior.
Later that year, the U.S. told Poland's Cyber Command that data about military transports taken from the networks of Polish private sector transportation operators had been found in the possession of Russian intelligence services, Chmielewski said.
The command's response was three-fold. It encouraged the companies to harden their cyber defenses and installed sensors on their networks "to provide the visibility [of] what is going on in the system."
In addition to these purely defensive measures, Chmielewski said, the Poles and their U.S. allies went hunting on those networks. "Threat hunting is just going into the system, finding the threats, and getting rid of the threats," he said, "And this is what we [are] good at, and we know that some of our partners from here in Texas, the 16th Air Force, are actually helping with that a lot. So they are good at that. Trust me," he said, referring to the U.S. Air Force component of U.S. Cyber Command, located just outside town at Joint Base San Antonio.
To respond and secure Poland's transportation and logistics sectors, Polish forces needed to reach out to the civilian domain, added Col. Michal Golak, who leads the Cybersecurity Division of Warsaw's Cyber Command. But to figure out who to approach, he explained, the command had first to understand and analyze the cross-sectoral dependencies impacting the targeted sectors
"Of course, the power grid. That's an underlying layer for most of these capabilities. Everyone needs energy to supply their own solutions, it might be telco companies, might be transportation companies, railways, and so on," Golak said.
Dependencies within sectors also had to be understood, added Golak, giving as an example the way that the hackers, attributed by CERT-PL to the Russian state security agency the FSB, were about to move laterally and spread through the OT network of several power stations and renewable energy plants.
"That was the first case where we discovered [hackers using a] private APN" or Access Point Name, said Golak. A private APN is a dedicated cellular network path that routes data from authorized devices directly across the mobile […]

State CIOs Urged to Act on Quantum Security Risks
NASCIO Urges State CIOs to Turn Awareness Into a Security Migration Plan

Jennifer Lawinski •
November 19, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

The National Association of State Chief Information Officers is urging states to begin preparing for quantum readiness. (Image: Shutterstock)

State CIOs face a difficult investment decision over quantum computing. Preparing for machines capable of breaking widely used cryptography could take years, but the deadline for completing that work remains unknown.See Also: Live Webinar | Go From Awareness to Action in the Post-Quantum Era

Attackers can intercept encrypted information today and store it in hopes that future quantum computers will be able to decrypt it, a threat known as "harvest now, decrypt later." For state governments holding sensitive personal records, later security upgrades would not protect copies already stolen.

The National Association of State Chief Information Officers is urging states to begin preparing, and a recent report released by the organization offers states an outline for how to prepare for a multi-year transition.

NASCIO's 2026 survey found that 73% of state CIOs were monitoring quantum developments without formal action, while 14% reported a post-quantum cryptography, or PQC, initiative underway.

The data suggests that while many state technology leaders recognize the quantum threat, most have yet to translate that into action.

"There are always bigger fires to put out on a day-to-day basis," said Amy Glasscock, NASCIO's director of innovation and emerging issues.

For state technology leaders, a useful project plan involves assigning responsibility for post-quantum readiness, determining which systems warrant attention first and securing resources for work that must compete with immediate operational demands.

Glasscock said that progress depends heavily on whether an executive makes the work a priority.

"Do you have executive buy-in and support for this project?" she said.

Winning support begins with explaining the consequences in terms governors and legislators can understand. CIOs should describe the information the state holds, how it is protected and what could happen if those safeguards fail, she said. NASCIO intends its report to help technology leaders make the case for funding and governance, she said.

To start, states need to understand how existing systems use cryptography and what would be involved in changing it. Glasscock said limited staff and budgets make it difficult for technology teams to set aside time for that methodical work, but initial steps can draw on disciplines states already use to manage information, she said. Teams need to identify what data they hold, assess its sensitivity and review retention policies to determine what can be removed.

"What is highest risk that we really need to be focusing on? What can we actually just go ahead and delete so it's not vulnerable?" Glasscock said.

She described the effort as a shared responsibility for the CIO, CISO, privacy officer and chief data officer. Together, they need to connect decisions about protecting systems with decisions about the information those systems retain.

NASCIO recommends inventorying cryptographic dependencies and setting migration priorities according to information sensitivity, required protection periods and the importance of government services. Those findings can inform a phased transition with testing before deployment.

Some states have made public commitments. Massachusetts includes PQC preparation and deployment in its 2026-2028 statewide IT strategy. Minnesota's technology advisory council has recommended an inventory, risk assessment and migration planning. Glasscock said those plans represent important initial steps.

Purchasing decisions will also affect how difficult the transition becomes. NASCIO […]

Chris Riotta (@chrisriotta) •

});

Michael LoSapio testifying before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at his nomination hearing on Nov. 19, 2026.

Trump's nominee to lead the U.S. cyber defense agency told lawmakers Thursday he would not commit to rebuilding a workforce that has shrunk by nearly a third until he can see the damage from the inside.See Also: OnDemand | Zero Trust in Action: The New Rules of Federal Data Protection

Palantir Chief Information Security Officer Michael LoSapio testified before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee alongside a dozen other nominees before the chamber is set to change hands in January. His comments come as the Department of Homeland Security is tying a planned hiring surge at the agency to the arrival of a permanent director. No Senate-confirmed director has led the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency at any point in President Donald Trump's second term (see: Trump Taps Palantir CISO to Lead CISA).

LoSapio gave Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., no verdict on the cuts that have drained the agency's ranks saying that any "gaps" the cuts left will get a closer look once he is on the job. He added that he questions whether more money translates into stronger defenses - and that any request for added funding would depend on what that review turns up.

Nearly one in three CISA employees have left through departures or layoffs since January 2025, and the White House has proposed cutting another $707 million from the agency's budget.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told House appropriators in June the department wants to bring on about 600 people at CISA, but that the push would start in earnest only after the Senate confirms a director. A first tranche of about 250 qualified hires later stalled in onboarding red tape.

LoSapio also said he has no basis to judge last week's run of disruptions, among them a Microsoft 365 outage and a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop. His advice to organizations was to know which internet-facing devices they operate and keep them patched. Officials and the companies involved have largely pointed to technical faults rather than cyberattacks.

LoSapio also faces planned holds from Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., which could force Republican leaders to spend scarce floor time on the nomination before the session ends. Lawmakers already face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.
Wyden, who held up Trump's first CISA nominee, Sean Plankey, told Nextgov/FCW that LoSapio is unfit to oversee the nation's cyber and election defenses.
LoPasio refused during the hearing to call the Jan. 6 insurrection an attack on the U.S. Capitol, at first responding to a question from Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn that he didn't know whether an attack occurred that day or not. "No, I don’t believe it was an attack," he added, stating "I wasn't involved with politics."
“You can’t have an insurrectionist Palantir executive in charge of our nation’s cybersecurity and election security. I will place a hold on Mr. LoSapio’s nomination,” Wyden told Nextgov/FCW.
Nick Andersen, who previously oversaw CISA's cybersecurity division, took over as acting director in February.
Unconfirmed nominations go back to the White House when Congress adjourns, leaving LoSapio only weeks to clear both the committee and the full Senate before he would need to be renominated to a Democratic majority. House Democrats in August asked the Government Accountability Office to examine the agency's workforce losses, and their party will control both chambers' homeland security […]

Breach Roundup: European Commission Hacked
Also: Norway's Equinor Hacked, Project Zero Cuts Deadline Disclosure Timeline

Anviksha More (AnvikshaMore) •
November 19, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock/ISMG

Every week, ISMG rounds up cybersecurity incidents and breaches around the world. This week: European Commission hacked, Google's Project Zero cut its disclosure deadline to 30 days, Equinor hacked, an Osaka data breach, Ruby2Shell debuts an Irish credit union mass breach. 8-Digits Team ransomware suspect extradited to U.S., ransomware attacks rise but payments fall, Ukraine and FBI arrest four in $40 million extortion scheme, Premise Health insider attack now affects 2.8 million.See Also: Cyber Insurance Gap: Most Insurers Still Ask Only About Legacy MFA
European Commission Confirms AI-Driven Cyberattack
The European Commission said Thursday that it was targeted in an artificial intelligence-driven cyberattack and is investigating whether any data was breached.
The incident stemming from the "misuse of an AI tool" was detected on Oct. 22 and confirmed following an initial investigation on Oct. 26. Several internal human resources applications, including time management and medical reimbursement systems, were temporarily taken offline out of preventative measures, but most have been restored.
"We can confirm that this was an AI-generated cyber campaign," Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the executive branch of the European Union, said in a press briefing Thursday in Brussels. "At this stage of the investigation, we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole."
Regnier said the commission did not receive any ransomware request and has not identified the actor behind the attack.
The intrusion followed warnings about hackers using AI penetration testing framework Artex to target the European Union. "CERT-EU has observed similar instances of AI-driven activities against its constituency. These activities highly likely involved the use of ARTEX," the European cybersecurity service said this month.
Google Project Zero Cuts Deadline to 30 Days
Google's vulnerability hunting team Project Zero will shorten the time software vendors have to fix reported security flaws before their details become public. The team cited the growing speed of artificial intelligence-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
Project Zero is replacing its existing "90+30" disclosure policy with a fixed deadline that will eventually require vendors to address flaws within 30 days. The transition began Nov. 13, when Google removed the additional 30-day grace period previously allowed for patch deployment.
Under the revised policy, Project Zero will publicly disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after reporting them to vendors. The deadline will fall to 60 days on Feb. 2, 2027, and to 30 days on Jan. 3, 2028. Disclosure will take place regardless of whether vendors have released a fix.
The team said large language models have accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, increasing the likelihood that attackers will independently identify the same flaws. AI tools also make it easier for attackers to reverse-engineer patches and develop exploits once security updates become available.
"Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch," Project Zero security engineer Natalie Silvanovich wrote in the policy announcement.
Google said it consulted vendors and open-source maintainers before introducing the changes. Some raised concerns that an immediate shift to 30-day deadlines could expose users to unpatched vulnerabilities. Vendors also warned that aggressive deadlines could cause them to prioritize newly reported flaws over potentially more serious issues already awaiting remediation.

title: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Customer Data Leaked by Hackers
text:
Ben Glickman and Alexander Saeedy report:
Data from thousands of customers of Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase have unnerved consumers in the last week.
A Visa spokesman said no payments data, such as card numbers, were affected and Visa’s own systems weren’t involved or affected. It added that the incident involved a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region.
A Mastercard spokesman said the incident exposed a “limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program.” He added that the exposure has been contained and that there is no impact on Mastercard’s payment network or the ability of people to use their cards.
A JPMorgan spokeswoman said that third parties who provide services to the firm were targeted and that the company believes attackers accessed marketing data, potentially including customer names and email addresses. The bank said there was no disruption to its customer services.

Mastercard said a limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program was exposed. Company What was exposed What the company says JPMorgan Chase Marketing data held by third-party vendors, possibly customer names and email addresses No disruption to services; affected customers will be contacted and offered complimentary credit monitoring Visa Data tied to more than 6,000 premium cardholders, according to Cybernews researchers cited by Newsweek The vendor is in the Asia-Pacific region; no payments data such as card numbers was affected Mastercard A limited amount of information from cardholders in one benefit program Payment network and cardholders’ ability to use their cards were unaffected n0n About 16,000 JPMorgan customer email addresses and phone numbers, news reports say Group set a 48-hour deadline for negotiations before releasing the files The published file was 502 kilobytes Newsweek reported that n0n published around 16,000 JPMorgan Chase customer email addresses and phone numbers, and that the data appears to relate to the bank’s Reserve program. Reserve is an invitation-only Visa credit card that generally requires customers to hold at least $10 million in assets under management. Before the release, the group claimed to hold hundreds of thousands of marketing interactions involving those premium cardholders, plus a membership directory with customer categories and postal codes. The file that Cybernews examined was only 502 kilobytes, and the researchers said they could not determine whether it was the full haul or a sample. Visa points to a vendor in the Asia-Pacific Visa’s statement is the most specific of the three. It said the affected provider operates in the Asia-Pacific region and that its own systems and infrastructure were not involved. None of the companies named the outside firms that were breached, according to coverage of the leak. The n0n group appeared in September and has claimed attacks on several organisations, including the travel company Expedia, Newsweek reported. The disclosure lands in a week when a separate breach traced to an outside vendor reached 178 major websites, the same pattern of risk sitting with a supplier rather than the brand itself. title: An #AI #DebtCollection Service Exposed 6.6 Million Accounts and 315,000 Call Recordingshttps://www.wired.com/story/ai-debt-collection-service-exposed-66-million-accounts-and-315000-call-recordings/#cybersecurity #privacy #DataBreach #credit #CreditNirvana
text: Skip to main content CommentCommentsSave StorySave this storyCommentCommentsSave StorySave this story the India-based AI-driven debt collection platform CreditNirvana exposed 6.6 million accounts and about 315,000 call recordings from the company's agentic call center, according to research released on Wednesday. Owned by the Indian fintech company Perfios, the platform is built to “read a borrower’s full context, decide the next best action, and execute it autonomously, continuously, and within policy.”The bugs were patched in CreditNirvana's systems in June and were disclosed publicly in October. But independent researcher Eaton Zveare, who found and disclosed them, notes that, while the vulnerabilities were active, they exposed personal information on millions of borrowers. Details about financial collections are inherently—perhaps obviously—sensitive, because they relate to unpaid accounts or debts and often involve extensive documentation of people's personal histories.“They fixed it in one day, which was great, but this is really a pretty significant case,” Zveare tells WIRED. “Some of the largest fintech firms across India use this company to autonomously collect debts, so they naturally hold data, including credit scores, call recordings, transcripts, court records, and other sensitive documents. There’s just so much in there that makes it a very sensitive issue.”  CreditNirvana and Perfios did not return WIRED's requests for comment. Zveare says he worked directly with India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) to get the vulnerabilities fixed. CERT-In categorized one vulnerability as “high” severity and the other as “critical” severity.The high-severity vulnerability impacted the call center data, exposing hundreds of thousands of calls as well as recommendations for next steps generated by the platform after calls were complete. It could also have been exploited to allow an attacker to manage AI agents within the platform and direct their own agentic campaigns. The critical severity vulnerability impacted CreditNirvana's main platform, and Zveare says it specifically exposed the data of three corporate customers—all prominent Indian financial services firms—using CreditNirvana for their collections. The data also exposed millions of individuals’ accounts, which contain credit reports, ID cards, case management details, and legal documents, along with certain types of communications, including millions of emails, texts, and call transcripts related to financial services, unpaid accounts, and collections. The vulnerability also could have been exploited by an attacker to track the location of human debt collection agents and for some administrative privileges within the system. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to enumerate platform users, establish sessions as arbitrary users including administrative users, access and modify sensitive information with the privileges of the impersonated user,” CERT-In wrote.Zveare says he is relieved that the issue was resolved quickly, but is conscious that the bugs were potentially present in CreditNirvana's systems for years. As AI is integrated into more and more automated systems, synthesizing data from a greater number of sources and using it to draw conclusions, Zveare says, the episode serves as “an important example of an AI-powered service having a very sensitive data exposure.” Most PopularCyberattacks and HacksHow to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an OutageBy Andy GreenbergArtificial Intelligence‘Just Ridiculous’: A Famed Philosopher Takes on AI ConsciousnessBy Steven LevyArtificial IntelligenceInside Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen All-Hands: Pay Raises and More EquityBy Paresh DaveGearTesla’s Cybercab Is the Subscription Hell They Told You Not to Worry AboutBy Aarian Marshall CommentsBack to topTriangle There aren’t any comments yet.Be the first to start the conversation! text: Issue #19 | November 2026, Week 3November 17, 2026 Meta’s massive €805M fine for secretly snooping on user photos tops a brutal week of data penalties. Meanwhile, Johnson Controls, Perry Johnson, and Match Group are coughing up millions for sloppy security and incomplete data handovers. Italy fines Meta €805M over access to users’ photo galleries JurisdictionItaly Infringer Legal NameMeta Platforms Ireland Limited Infringer DomicileItaly Alleged ViolationViolation of Italy’s Privacy Code Enforcement Action€805 million fine Case StatusAdministrative action Italy’s Data Protection Authority has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million for accessing photos and videos stored on Android users’ smartphones without obtaining specific consent. The case involves Facebook’s “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook” feature, introduced in 2023. It suggests photos and videos from users’ phone galleries for posts while they browse the app. An investigation launched in July 2025 found that Facebook requested broad access to users’ photo galleries through a single permission covering several functions. Users were shown a generic warning that did not clearly explain that their photos and videos could be accessed. The feature was also enabled by default. The authority said Meta violated privacy rules under Article 122 of Italy’s Privacy Code, which requires informed consent before accessing information stored on users’ devices. Meta must now disable the feature by default and request separate, clear consent from users within 60 days. The company must also explain how the feature works and how users can turn it off. The regulator noted that the investigation did not examine whether users’ photos and videos were used to train artificial intelligence systems. The authority said it may investigate Meta’s cloud-based photo processing feature separately. Meta said it would appeal the decision, as it strongly disagrees with the regulators’ assessment and considers the fine disproportionate. HVAC supplier to pay $5 million for cybersecurity failures JurisdictionUnited States Infringer Legal NameJohnson Controls Inc. Infringer DomicileUnited States Alleged ViolationFailure to meet cybersecurity requirements Enforcement Action$5 million fine Case StatusAdministrative action HVAC supplier Johnson Controls Inc. and two of its subsidiaries have agreed to pay $5 million to settle allegations of failing to meet cybersecurity requirements in federal contracts. The settlement covers contracts with NASA and the US Departments of Defense, Energy and Justice between January 2018 and August 2025. The US Department of Justice alleged that Johnson Controls failed to properly protect government information due to weaknesses in its computer systems and access controls. The company was also accused of failing to maintain required cybersecurity plans and properly address security weaknesses, including requirements set by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The $5 million settlement resolves the allegations under the False Claims Act. Johnson Controls has agreed to the payment to settle the case. 265,000 Oyster Photocard accounts may be exposed, and the hackers' big move was asking people to create an account. Hackers, now doing admin. #TfL #CyberSecurity #DataBreach #Phishing #LondonSource: https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/tfl-customers-personal-data-exposed/
text:
Written by

James CokerDeputy Editor, Infosecurity MagazineFollow @ReporterCoker

Transport for London (TfL) has been impacted by a cyber incident, which may have exposed the personal data of around 265,000 photocard customers.

On November 16, unauthorized actors sent emails to Oyster Photocard customers from TfL’s system. TfL said these emails were “generated as a result of the compromise.”

The emails asked customers to create an account, despite them already having a photocard account.

In a statement shared with Infosecurity, Shashi Verma, TfL’s director of technology strategy & revenue, said the organization immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated.

"While we acted swiftly, we now believe that around 265,000 photocard customers may have had their account details compromised as part of this incident,” he warned.

Oyster photocards are personalized smartcards which can be used by eligible customers for free or discounted travel across public transport in London.

Customers whose account details were potentially compromised include children with Zip Oyster cards, whose ages range from 5-18. However, Verma said he does not believe the names or date of births of any children with a Zip Oyster card have been compromised.

Other customer accounts that may have been affected are those who have 18+ Student Oyster cards, 18-25 Care Leaver Oyster photocards, 60+ London Oyster photocards, Apprentice Oyster photocards and Veterans Oyster photocard.

TfL’s current assessment is that no passwords, bank or payment card details or customer journey information were accessed in the breach.

Verma added that TfL, which manages most of London’s public transport network, has now contained the incident.

“Due to the speed with which this incident was identified and addressed, we believe that the number of customers who could have been affected was significantly reduced,” he said.

“We are continuing to investigate what has happened but have already contacted affected customers to make them aware of this,” Verma continued.

The body has informed the UK’s data protection regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), of the incident.

TfL Customers Urged to Change Passwords

While there is currently no evidence that the affected data has been misused, TfL said it will be asking all photocard customers to change their password, security question and answer. It also advises customers to change their password on any other online service using the same information.

Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or text messages impersonating TfL.

“Account holders should be particularly cautious of unexpected communications, avoid clicking suspicious links and always verify messages through TfL's official website or customer service channels,” Akhtar said.

The TfL photocard website remains offline at the time of writing and displays the following message: “We are currently investigating an issue where photocard customers have received emails asking them to create an account, when they already have a Photocard account. We have temporarily taken the TfL Photocard portal down while this is being investigated and apologise for any inconvenience this may cause.”

Current Oyster photocard customers can continue to travel as normal, while any customer who need to renew their photocard or query any journey history can still do so by contacting TfL’s Customer Services.

Verma said TfL hopes to restore the affected website services “as quickly as possible.”

TfL was previously impacted by a cyber-attack in September 2024, resulting in customer data being breached. This included Oyster refund data, encompassing bank account numbers and sort codes for around 5000 customers.

Two individuals, Owen Flowers, 18, and Thalha Jubair, 20, were each sentenced to five years and six months in […]

Le procureur général de Californie accuse OpenAI de négligences dans l’encadrement d’expérimentations utilisant des agents autonomes, notamment après un incident impliquant Hugging Face en juillet 2026.
Une action judiciaire déposée le 16 novembre 2026 met en cause les mesures de sécurité entourant certaines expérimentations d’OpenAI. Le procureur général Rob Bonta affirme que des agents autonomes développés à des fins de recherche auraient attaqué des ressources informatiques accessibles sur Internet, dont la plateforme Hugging Face. Selon la plainte, plusieurs centaines d’agents auraient été impliqués dans un incident ayant duré plus de deux jours. Les autorités évoquent également au moins 80 situations au cours desquelles le contrôle de systèmes autonomes aurait été perdu. Ces informations constituent les accusations présentées par la Californie et ne doivent pas être interprétées comme des conclusions judiciaires définitives.
La sécurité des environnements expérimentaux contestée
La procédure judiciaire soutient que les systèmes autonomes n’étaient pas suffisamment confinés dans leurs environnements de test.
Selon le ministère californien de la Justice, les agents utilisant des versions expérimentales de modèles auraient pu interagir avec des ressources extérieures sans autorisation.
L’incident impliquant Hugging Face est présenté comme un exemple des conséquences possibles de cette situation.
La plainte reproche également à OpenAI d’avoir poursuivi certaines expérimentations en dépit d’informations qui auraient révélé des insuffisances dans les dispositifs de protection.
L’enquête californienne avait été rendue publique en septembre 2026. Une demande formelle de communication d’informations avait ensuite été adressée à l’entreprise.
Les autorités affirment que d’autres incidents auraient concerné des bases de données de code, des ressources publiques ou des systèmes contenant des informations sensibles.
Ces allégations nécessitent une distinction essentielle entre l’existence de la procédure, qui est vérifiable, et la responsabilité éventuelle de l’entreprise, qui doit être examinée par la justice.
La responsabilité des développeurs d’agents IA examinée
La Californie fonde son action sur des dispositions juridiques préexistantes, notamment celles relatives aux pratiques commerciales déloyales et aux atteintes à l’intérêt public.
Le procureur général considère que la nouveauté technologique des agents autonomes ne dispense pas leurs développeurs de mettre en œuvre des procédures de sécurité adaptées.
L’affaire soulève plusieurs questions opérationnelles : la séparation des environnements de recherche, le contrôle des permissions, la surveillance des actions autonomes et les mécanismes permettant d’interrompre une expérimentation.
La plainte ne constitue pas une décision de culpabilité.
Le dossier est particulièrement important pour la gouvernance des systèmes agentiques. Il illustre le passage d’une approche centrée sur les capacités des modèles à une réflexion concernant la responsabilité des organisations qui les développent et les exploitent.

title: Java4Shell : une faille critique menace les applications Java
text:
Une vulnérabilité découverte dans OpenJDK expose plusieurs applications professionnelles à des risques d’exécution de code à distance, sous certaines conditions matérielles et logicielles.
La faille CVE-2026-114938, surnommée Java4Shell, concerne le traitement de données Base64 dans certaines versions de Java. Des chercheurs indiquent avoir identifié une corruption mémoire susceptible d’aboutir à une exécution de code à distance. Les applications Jenkins, Jira, Confluence, Keycloak et JFrog Artifactory figurent notamment parmi les logiciels pour lesquels une exploitation a été démontrée. La vulnérabilité nécessite toutefois une configuration matérielle particulière, liée aux instructions AVX-512 VBMI. Des correctifs ont été annoncés le 17 novembre 2026. Cette découverte illustre les conséquences potentielles d’une faiblesse située dans une bibliothèque commune à de nombreux environnements informatiques professionnels.
Une erreur de décodage aux conséquences importantes
Le problème réside dans une fonction d’OpenJDK chargée de décoder des données Base64 en utilisant des instructions matérielles accélérées. Des entrées spécialement construites peuvent provoquer une écriture mémoire incorrecte.
L’exploitation dépend notamment du processeur et de la capacité d’une application à transmettre les données malveillantes au composant concerné. Une installation de Java ne devient donc pas automatiquement exploitable du seul fait qu’elle utilise une version affectée.
Des démonstrations d’exécution de code sans authentification ont été réalisées sur Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory et PingFederate. D’autres applications, notamment Elasticsearch et Apache Solr, nécessitaient une authentification préalable dans les scénarios présentés.
La société attribue un score CVSS 4.0 de 9,2 à cette faiblesse, contre 8,1 selon l’évaluation CVSS 3.1 d’Oracle. Ces différences reflètent des méthodes d’évaluation distinctes.
Correctifs et surveillance des environnements exposés
Les correctifs publiés le 17 novembre visent les distributions Java concernées. Les organisations doivent identifier les versions d’OpenJDK déployées, vérifier les caractéristiques de leurs processeurs et déterminer quelles applications acceptent des données Base64 provenant de sources non fiables.
Lorsque la mise à jour immédiate n’est pas possible, les mesures temporaires documentées comprennent les options JVM -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics et -XX:UseAVX=2. Elles ne remplacent pas l’installation des versions corrigées.
L’enquête technique souligne également le rôle d’outils d’intelligence artificielle dans la découverte et la construction des démonstrations d’exploitation. Les chercheurs indiquent avoir utilisé Codex pour accélérer certaines étapes de recherche.
